div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
JACK: " There are more women than men in the world." Tom: "Yea; but there are enough women who want to be men to balance matters."

FIRST STATESMAN: "I can truly say that n man ever sought to bribe me." Second Ditto "Oh, well, I wouldn't be discouraged. Your luck may change some time or other." "DEAR father, we are all well and happy. The baby has grown ever so much and has a great deal more sense than he used to have. Hoping the same of you, I remain your daughter Molly." -- • -

"I HEAR that Jigson holds quite a responsible position, and that he is financially interested in the concern he is with." " Yes ; they owe me six months' salary." LrrirLit BETH (in the country) : " Grandpapa, you must have to keep an awful lot of policemen out here." Grandpapa : "Why, Beth?" "Oh, there's such a lot of grass to keep off of!" FIRST LADY (off for a journey): "I hope we've got the right train." Second Lady: "I asked seventeen porters and ninety-three passengers if this train went to Manchester, and every one said Yes,' so I think we're all right." A COUNTRY newspaper correspondent recently sent this cheerful bit of news to his paper "Brooks is at last provided with a nice hearse, and our citizens can now be conveyed to their graves in comfort. This is something that has long been needed here." "BUT, Emma, how can you prefer the plain and shabbily-dressed Julius to my elegant and hand- some brother ? " "That is quite simple ; your brother is in love with himself, and Julius with me." PLAUSIBLE. —Little Johnny: "Aunt Julia, what makes those funny spots on your face ? " Aunt Julia (who is very freckled): " I believe it's because I have so much iron in my blood; it is only when I have been out in wet weather, tholfgh, that they are noticeable." Little Johnny: "Oh, yes; I know. You got out in the weather and the iron in your blood gets rusted." AN ELABORATE TEST. —Mother (suddenly com- ing upon her daughter as she is terminating a love-letter with these words: "I take you at your word; I love you, and will continue to love you while life shall last !") : "What does this mean, Amelia?" Emancipated School-girl: "Nothing, mamma. I was only trying a pen ; " "WE have a lovely whist club," she said, art- lessly. "We made a rule that any girl who spoke should pay a penny into the treasury for every word she uttered." "Quite ingenious." " Yes ; but I don't belong to it any more." "Why not?" "Pa says he can't afford it." MEDICAL ADVICE.—" You see your wife ought to take a great deal more exercise." "But, doctor, what am Ito do? She never will go out." "Oh ! that is very easily remedied. Give her some money and tell her to go a-shopping." HEROIC REMEDY. —Di s tressed Young Mother (with crying baby in railway carriage): "Dear, dear! I don't know whatever to do with this child !" Kind and Thoughtful Bachelor (on the opposite seat) : " Shall I open the window for you, madam?" NOT A GOOD BARGAIN.—The eyes of the suitor filled with tears. "Sir,'' he protested, "I would give my very life for your daughter." Her father started violently, "Young man," he thundered, "do I look as if I might be easily cheated in a bargain?" Before his gaze the youth averted his face, abashed. AT THE SODA FOUNTAIN. Clerk: "What flavour?" Bridget (aside to Pat) : " Phat do he mean, Pat?" Pat: "Whist, Biddy, don't show yer igerance ; they has fruit flavours in the soda. I'll be havin' strawberry in mine." Bridget: "Oh, yis, Oi see, fruit flavours; Oi'll have onion in mine."

"How did you come to hit the plaintiff?" said the counsel o the prisoner. "Come to hit 'im, is it? Why, man, dear, your honour, I wasn't two fut from him, and I couldn't have missed hittin' him if I had been cross eyed."

CANDID. —Doctor : "Your wife is in a very critical state, mid I should recommend you to call in some specialist to consult on the case." Husband: "There, you see doctor, I was right again! I told my wife long ago she ought to get proper medical advice, but she always thought you might be offended !"

NEW WIFE : "To-morrow is your birthday, darling, and I am going to stop at the jeweller's and buy you a present." Her Hubby: "Get something cheap, pet; I haven't paid him for my Christmas present yet." W ATCHFUL OTHER. : "Have you complied with my wishes and informed Mr. Busses that he can have but one kiss when he says good night?" Dutiful Daughter : "Yes, ma." "And how does it affect him ?" "He says it much earlier and oftener than he used to."
RIGGLE : " What did Miss Dawson say when you broke off your engagement with her?" Twaggle : "She didn't say anything; she was speechless." Riggle : "Good gracious ! What a wife you've missed !" . _ _

INQIRING PERSON : "What time did the hotel catch fire?" Fireman: "Midnight." Inquiring Person: "Everybody got out safe?" Fireman: "All except the night watchman. They couldn't wake him up in time." "You have a lively set of clerks," he said to the proprietor of the establishment. "It, must be pleasant and profitable to have employs so full of energy and enthusiasm." "Yes," responded the proptietor ; "we close early to-day, and they are getting ready to go home." LITTLE EDITH had just been to church for the first time. "And what did you think of it?" asked her mother. "I didn't like the organ very well," she replied. "Why not?" "Tause there wasn't any monkey with it!" A THOROUH BUSINESS MAN.—Optician (to his new shopman) : "When you send out the price lists, write the addresses as small as possible, so that the customers may see that it is time they began to wear glasses." "JOHN," called out Mrs. Billus, "are you ready to put up those new curtain fixtures?" "I am beginning to put them up now, Maria," was the response that came, in a metallic tone of voice, Irmo the parlour. "Children," said Mrs. BMus, with nervous haste, " run out and play !" "I SUPPOSE you know," said the indulgent parent to the anxious suitor, "that my daughter has been reared in the lap of luxury?" "Yes, sir, I know that. Still, lam glad you realise the importance of making us a liberal allowance to live upon." tiscLx : "When you find that you've made a mistake, start again right where you we're before and try to do better." Nephew: "Thank you, sir. I've made a mistake of spending that five. pound note you gave me two weeks ago. Please give me another, so I can start where I was before."

RECTOR'S WIFE . "You ought to avoid even the appearance of evil. Do you yourself think the girls who dance are right?" Eelle of the Parish : "They must be. I know the girls who don't dance are always left." A CAREFUL FATHER. —" Look here," said the parent to the school teacher, "I see that one of the lines in my boy's copybook is Less haste, more speed.'" " Yes." " Awl here's another that reads, 'The longest way lound is the shortest way hr‘rne.' " " Yes." "Well, I want it stopped. I don't want those out-of-date proverbs festooned around his intellect. I'm educating him for business." LICKED INTO FITS. —" I can tell you something that you haven't got," said a German to an American. "We have built a church so long that it takes half an hour to walk from the porch to the pulpit." " That is nothing!" replied the Yr.,nkee. " We have a church where a little boy is carried to his baptism through the east porch, and at the west porch he walks cut as a minister with his aehnnd wife." UNDRESSING MADE EASY.—A gentleman who, near the close of the last century, accompanied Baron Von Swieton on a visit to the old Duke of Sachsen-flidburghausen relates the following in his memoirs: "The Duke regularly goes to bed every night at eight o'clock. When leaving the sitting. room to proceed to his rather distant sleeping apartment, he has a number of his valets posted all along the line of route. One of them takes possession of his wig, the secoud divests him of his coat, and so on, until, by the time he has reached the goal, he is ready to slip into bed with- out more ado."

While at Lowther Castle, during the temporary absence of his host, the Earl of Lonsdale,the Kaiser caused his own servants to unpack a heavy case, which proved to contain a very fine marble bust of his Imperial Majesty, which he then screened by means of a large palm. On Lord Lonsdale's return be withdrew the palm, and to his lordship's sur- prise, there stood the beautiful sculpture, which was then formally presented to Lord Lonsdale,who was greatly delighted with it. The Emperor was so delighted with the arrangements for his recep- tion at Penrith that he sent £5O to be distributed amongst the poor in winter, or during any period of privation. The Kaiser also left the servants at Lowther £l5O, and to the railway servants .£5O; while he forwarded a diamond ring to the chief of the telegraph service.

The Rev. Lecnard Isitt, the notable New Zealand reformer, who is now in England, is responsible, more than anyone else, for the drastic liquor legis- lation which was recently carried in that colony. Mr. lsitt is a Methodist minister, and for some time his conference has granted him special facilities for carrying on political work, and he has taken his place at the bead of the reformers of the colony. In spite of his clerical dress, he looks something like a prize-tighter, with his bullet-shaped, pugnacious- looking head, and strong frame. He is an emphatic and fluent speaker, and has great power in arous- ing the feelings of the most phlegmatic assemblies.

It is not certain whether Mr. Talbot or Lord Cran • borne will be chairman of the Church party. In any case the party undoubtedly means business,and I bear that some thirty or forty of the new mem- bers have been invited to join its ranks. ltsattitude is to be " entirely independent " of the official leaders, and it will promote several measures in the course of next session, including probably one deal- ing with the cases of incumbents who neglect the work of their parishes. It is held by some of the Church reformers that on matters of discipline the bishop ought to be able to deprive an incumbent of his living not merely for breaches of the moral law, but also for incompetency and neglect. The whole question of patronage is also to be gone into.

It is considered in some quarters not impossible that Mr. John Morley may resume his duties as " reader" to the firm of Macmillan. Even should Mr. Morley decline to re-enter politics he will have left a name to posterity (remarks a London corres- pondent) as the only Cabinet Minitser who ever possessed sufficient moral courage to have his front door opened to visitors by a parlour-maid, London was the scene of this innovation ; when Mr. Morley went to live at the Chief Secretary's Lodge in Phcenix Park he became reconciled to a butler,foot- men, and other paraphernalia of vice-regaiism.

Dr. Tanner's suspension has deprived him of the privilege of serving on any of the committees. This is part of the penalty which accompanies the sus- pension, and it happens that it has disabled him from sitting on the Kitchen Committee. The doctor is one of the whips of the Anti-Parnellite party, and he put down his own name for election on the committee. The suspension came before the committee was appointed, and another Irish name was promptly substituted in the place of the doctor's, to the great comfort, no doubt, of both the Unionists and Liberals who compose the committee.

One of the most interesting series of experiments which have been carried on at Aldershot for some time past relates to the reconnoitring power of balloons. The authorities are not troubling them- selves about solving the knotty problem of steering balloons, which is left entirely in the hands of en- quiring outsiders. The obj.cts of the experiments refer chiefly to such practical questions as the number of aerial ascents that may be made by a balloon with one supply of gas merely, and the value of the balloon, under all atmospherieal con- ditions, for reconnoitring purposes. The aeronaut school at Aldershot was visited the other day by M. Andre, the adventurous gentleman who proposes next year to set out in a balloon in quest of the North Pole. Though he is already master of the art of ballooning, he was naturally anxious to learn everything that can he learned, and he was re- ceived by the Aldershot authorities with great cordiality. We in this country know little about the Aldershot school ; but its fame attracts great. numbers of Continental visitors who are interested both in ballooning and in war.

The meeting of the Radical Committee duly took place on Tuesday, but nothing of an authoritative character has been allowed to come out as to is proceedings. Whether secrecy is tet be definitely maintained or not is doubtful, but at all events the Committee are desirious cf maintaining silence for a few days. There appears to be little doubt that questions of organisation were under di-cos:4°n. It is rumoured, too—though the report must be taken with caution,—that there was some talk on the subject, of the party leadership. But this is in any case a question about which we are .to hear more in the early future. To put the matter plainly, there is supposed to have been a revival—or an at- tempt at a revival—in the last few days of certain intrigues in respect to the leadership, of which one heard more than enough in the last Parliament. There is no need to specify the quarters in which they are being promoted. It is evident that before the Liberal party can do really good work in the new Parliament all doubts on the question of alleg- iance must be brought to an end, and if controver- sies of this kind are inevitable the sooner they are frankly dealt with the better. It is known to every- body that the Unionist made great capital at the general election out of the supposed divided counsels in the Liberal leadership.'

The motion of which Lord CastMown has given notice in favour of the abolition of the Lord Lieu- tenancy will receive considerable backing in !be Upper House. The question will also be brought to the notice in the House of Commons early next session. It would have been discussed at the re- cent meeting of the Irish Unionists, but it was not thought worth while to enter on matters of policy in the course of the present short session. As soon as the House meets next year, however, the Irish Unionists who are in favour of the change will bring the matter forward, and a resolution some- what in the terms of Lord Castletown's will in all probability be at once placed on the paper. There is an idea in some quarters, however, that the Gov- ernment may frustrate the proposed agitation by promising some changes on the lines desired in the Queen's Speech. It is quite evident already that next session is bound to be to a very large extent an Irish session.

A little while ago, when the late Government were endeavouring to do something to make the county magistracy less one-sided and more repre- sentative than it is, we heard a good deal about the large fees usually exacted by the Clerks of therence for placing the new J.P.s on the Commission. At first, there was all manner of mystery as to what the fee was, and what it was for ; hut, point by point, it came out that it was no more than n pleasant usage, encouraged by the Clerks of the , Peace for obvious reasons, and submitted to by new 11 magistrates out of a fine conservative tradition. although there was really no reason why there should be any fee at all. Now, however, we learn with interest—and we confess with surprise—that the Clerk of the Pence for Huntingdon has actually summoned two of the recently appointed Liberal J.P.s before the County Court., because they do not see their way ta pay him ten guineas each for nothing in particular. We shell see what case the learned clerk will make. The fee cannot rest on "custom," for custom in the law must go back to Richard 11.. and it is quite clear that no such fee at all was paid then, and if there had been a fee, it would have been nearer to tenpence than to ten guineas. Neither can it. be what the law calls "quantum msruit," for the clerk has certainly not. performed either ten guineas' worth or 10n. worth of work. We do not know of any statutory anti,- erity for the exaction, and on public grounds, we shall'not be sorry to see the matter tried in court, and the law settled once for all.

IThe Rev. Hugh Price Hughes, writes a corresp,ii. dent, is spending a much-needed holiday, wir h Mr.. Hughes. whose energy is equal to that, of her hu-- band. in Switzerland. Mr. Hughes arrived at Grin- delwald on Wednesday last, and within two or three hours he was presiding at a lecture delivered in'the parish church by the Rev. Joseph Hocking. Mr. Hughes said, in the course of his remarks, that he feared the people of England were losing much ' of the local colour and interest which formerly did so much to foster clanship. Mr. Hughes, who looks eiready much better, was expected to preach at Grindelwald on Sunday. He has done some climb- ing on the lovely slopes facing the hotel where he is staying, opposite the Scheidegg.

The first Sister of Mercy to begin her work of love in California was Lord Russell of Killowen's sister.

Cases made of paper pulp, for preserved products, are in use as substitutes for the ordinary tin can. Window plants in Germany are often watered with cold tea or coffee. The effects are said to be beneficial. " How was it Mary Anne wasn't in church this morn- ing, Mrs. Murphy ?" " Faith, it wasn't the girl's fault, but hr big sleeves, Mrs. Gilhooly. There's room only for her lather an' her two big sistcrs in the pew till the fashions change." The kindly practice of embodying in the obituary announcement a list of the good qualities of the dead seems to find favour in Birmingham. The following appeared the other day in one of the lecal papers : • LOUGHTON. —On the sth inst., at his residence John Loughton,aged seventy-two years. He was Dever known to utter a wicked word, or be the worse for beer, though not an abstainer. A loving and devoted father to his motherless children for twenty-eight years. May he rest in peace ! Aluminium neckties have been introduced into Ger- many. They are really made of the cosmwelitan metal, and frosted or otherwise ornamented in various shapes imitating the ordinary silk or satin article. They are fastened to the collar-button by a band around the neck, and are particularly recommended for summer wear, since they can be easily cleaned when soiled, while they are not perceptibly heavier than cotton, cambric, or silk.

_ It has been discovered that ladieswho wish to heighten their complexions need no longer use paints and unguents that are injurious to the skin. " Blackberry er strawberry juice rubbed slightly on the cheeks and then washed off with milk gives a beautiful tint." "The garden beet is also an excellent cosmetic ; the beet is cut and the juice applied gently with a camel's-hair brush."

Mr. Alexander Campbell, of Charlotte Town, Prince Edward Island, has established a record. He is now in his eighty-fourth year, but on the fast Sunday in July he had the gratification of hearing that his better half had presented him with five daughters at a birth. So at least say the Canadian papers. In a cemetery in the suburbs of Lowell.Massachusctts, there are five headstones all alike, ex, ept thA inscrip- tions. The first one reads, " First wife of John Smith," and the second, " Second wife," and so on until the fifth stone, which reads, " John Smith ; at rest, at last." The marriage rate during the first quarter of this year was lower than any quarter on record, the figures bong only 10,6 of the adult population of England and Wales. The best districts for marriage were, of course, the in- dustral portions of the country. Northumberland heads the list, the marriages there in the three months being at the rate of 13.4 per thousand. The East Rioing of Yorkshire, South Wales, Lancashire, and Durham come next. In London the rate was 11 4,0 r one in 1,000 above the average of all England and Wales.

Brains in the Fingers. It may not be so generally known that recent post- mortem examinations of the bodies of the blind reveal the fact that the nerves at the ends of the fingers well. defin.d cells of grey matter had:formed,identical in sub- starce and in cell formation ot the grey matter of the bran. What does this show? It proves that a man can think not alone in his head, but all over his body, and especially in the great nerve centres like the solar plexus, and the nerve ends on the palm of the hands and the soles of the feet. The coming man will assuredly perceive and think in every part, from his head down to his feet.

French Babies. It is not generally known that in France it is forbidden under severe penalties,for anyone to give infants under one year any form of solid food, unless such be ordered by written prescription, signed by a legally qualified medical man. Nurses are also forbidden to use, in the rearing of infants confined to their care, at any time, or under any pretext whatever, any nursing bottle pro- vided with a rubber tube. Several other similar and equally stringent laws have recently been enacted by the French Government, which, despairing ot obtaining any increase in the birth-rate in their land, is now turning its attention to the saving of the few children that are born.

A Word on Eyebrows. We often fail to realise the beauty that lies in nicely- marked eyebrows. The aristocratic heroines of the novel- ettes have always"pencilled brows." The eyebrows soften and lend expression to b- th eyes and brows. However lovely the eyes may be in themselves, they are yet ineffective if the brows are scanty and irregular. When the eyebrows are thin and scattering they may be in- duced to grow by the application of camphorated oil. It must he applied by means of a brush where it is de- sired to have the hair grow. When the brows are lost by fire, they will grow again if a wash made from 5 grains of sulphate of quinine in an ounce of alcohol is used.

An Aged Bridegroom. According to an aist Anglian paper a Suffolk village has been much exercised over the marriage of an old couple aged seventy and seventy-two. The bridegroom was deaf and could not read, but he had been "Crammed " with the service; but, like many other crammed people, he broke down. " The parson and clerk shouted themselves hoarse, but he only gently shook his head and stared vacantly. The old woman tried her hand, or rather voice. She put her arms round his neck, her mouth to his 'ear, and shrieked in her quavery treble, •To h toe and to hold.' This was too much for the gravity of the congregation. They could restrain themselves no longer, and the stillness of that little church was broken by peals of laughter from young and old. The never-failing village blacksmith was called in, and with the aid of his stentorian voice a faint echo was conveyed to the old man's brain, who,at last, almost weeping, smiled and nodded his consent, which was considered sufficient.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAREST NELLIE,

Hats are as light and summery as possible just now, for in this hot weather we certainly do not wish to carry any superfluous weight on our heads. The light fancy straw shapes, with low crown and straight brim, trimmed with a profusion of flowers, are very generally becoming, and are so easy to trim too. The flowers are just arranged in a wreath round the crown, and the garnitures can be bought ready for sewing on. Those shapes are also trimmed with big rosettes and twists of net, white, blue, red, green, or shot, to suit the dress or fancy of the wearer, and these trimmings also are sold complete, so that even the girl who is least clever with her fingers can trim her own hats. A summer travelling hat is made in Panama straw, trimmed with white chiffon and white wings. This is very beooming to a youthful face.

Some of the simplest materials are being used for gowns, and there are some of them very striking. For instance, a well-known leader of fashion was seen the other in a dress of piqué! The piqué was a very good one, firm but not harsh, in a pale cafe-au-laid shade. The skirt was a godet model, decorated with two panels in front of white Madeira embroidery. The full blouse volts of cafe-au-lait lawn, with front and collar of Madeira embroidery and broad belt of broad chamois leather.

A race gown is of white crepon with coloured silk floral design in very delicate shades. The skirt is very full at the edge, with large pleats at the back. The corsage flou is a series of &yea- homes made in white silk muslin, very light and fleecy, with a large square yoke of point cle Venice. The sash, of superb Pompadour ribbon, rises like a pointed corselet in front and ties in a gigantic bow at the back. These sash bows are often so wide, and the loops are so distended (instead of falling softly) that the bow is plainly noticeable in front —protruding beyond the elbows in some exag- gerated cases. Sometimes these bows are of velvet or satin, not of ribbon at all; then the loops are considerably longer and wider than the ends, which taper off to a point. In some light outdoor dresses this bow and the puff sleeves are velvet or dark satin, affording an agreeable contrast. A pretty fête costume I saw recently had a print blouse with pink flowers on a white ground. A frill of fawn-coloured alpaca passed over the shoulders nearly to the waist, where was a knot of the same material with hanging ends. A pretty hat trimmed with trelle and grasses was also worn.

A particularly pretty sleeveless blouse can be made of dark blue Irish linen, with sailor collar of white linen, edged with three rows of very narrow gold braid, and having an effective arrangement of small gold buttons and loops in front. One and a-half yards of 30-inch blue linen and three- quarters of white is sufficient, or the blouse looks equally well in serge, with the collar of either linen, drill, white serge, or flannel. The design is an excellent one for utilising a short remnant of stuff. Here is another hint for using up a remnant of silk or pretty-tinted cloth. A dainty evening wrap can be made of but two and a-half yards of silk, or one and a-half of double-width cloth, and five-eighths of satin will cut the square collar, which is covered with lace. Two and a-half yards of wide cream combination lace will be required for the epaulettes and stoles, and one yard of a heavier design for the satin collar,

A very neat outdoor bodice is made of grey silk shot with green. There is a white silk vest, sur- mounted by green velvet collar fastened at one side; grey er6pon skirt, with silk lines of green running downwards. The large picture hat of black straw, surmounted by grey ostrich plumes. Your loving ... JENNIE.

LOVE'S CONFESSION. Touching the part which Lord James Fitzjames bad played in the battle it might be difficult to speak without prejudice. During the notes of pre- paration his voice had only been heard seeking in- formation as to the probabilities of escape from the pursuing freebooter. At the opening of the conflict he had been snugly ensconsed beneath the break of the poop, but, by some strange freak, a strange bullet found him in his place of ambuscade and lodged in the fleshy part of his forearm. With commendable alacrity he dodged into the cabin, making his way thence by a bulkhead passage to the cock-pit, where the sur- geon shortly afterwards found him. The bullet was extracted from his flesh, after which the wound was dressed. .

The surgeon informed Lord James that he might still be of great use on deck; but the peer con- cluded that he could be of sufficient service below decks to warrant his remaining. Lord James did his duty nobly in the cock-pit. While he could assist the surgeon in caring for the seriously wounded he forgot his own wound, and shrank not from the sight of blood which flowed from other's veins; but it turned out, however, that he had lost the good opinion of Mary, and he was not long in discovering that she held herself aloof from him. _ _ _
But to return to those who had borne the brunt of the battle. .. .

By one of those strange dispensations which so often befall the course of deadly conflict, he who had been most exposed—he who had led in the fight— he upon whom the arm of vengeance had aimed its fiercest blows—he who had struck down so many of the enemy, Arthur Rainsford,—had not even received a scratch. Capt. Harlow had received a alight sword-cut upon the shoulder, and Mr. Spencer had received a out upon the left arm and a slight thrust in the hip. Mr. Nixon, the second lieutenant, was in the sur- geon's hands; but his wound was not considered dangerous. It was early in the evening during the second dog-watch that Sir Jasper joined Arthur upon the quarter-deck. "Mr. Rainsford," said the old soldier, with deep feeling, "you need not shrink from me, for I am not going to ply you with any more laudations. I have something in mind of a more serious nature. Assuring you that I am sincere in desiring to promote your welfare, I trust you will be frank with me.' _ _
"YOU may command me, Sir Jasper." "I have told you that your father was my friend. I also knew your mother. She married with Lord Birchmear 1"

"Yes, sir." "And afterwards removed to England?" "They were married to England." "And you have been—" Arthur held up his hand and interrupted the 'speaker. "My dear Sir Jasper, you desire to know what my present relations are with Lord Birch- mear ?" .
"Yes, my boy. I desire it that I may know whether any offer of assistance from me would be acceptable to you." "You have not kept the run of Lord Birch- mear ?"

"I'll tell you how far, Arthur. I know him well. I knew him long before he married with your mother. I was in India when he returned after your mother's death, and I was in Calcutta when he took for his second wife the widow of Sir Theobald Travers. She—she—"
"Speak frankly, Sir Jasper." " Well, it's the truth. She made a conquest. She was as poor as a church mouse. Sir John sur- rendered at discretion." _ _
"Perhaps," said Arthur, "you knew that Lady Travers had a son " _ _ _

"Captain Harold Travers, of the Fortieth. I knew him. I had the pleasure of sitting in court- martial upon him on a certain occasion. And he followed his mother to Birchmear." " Yes ; and took the family name of Berwick." "Poor Sir John ! " muttered the old soldier.

After a pause Arthur spoke freely. He told to Sir Jasper, as far as he could with propriety, how the coming of the new Lady Birchmear and her son had affected himself. He was frank in telling how his own wayward course had given his enemies opportunities again him, and he closed by giving an account of the last unfortunate affair at Birch- wear. He was sure the trouble had been brewed beforehand for his injury. He told of the duel, omitting names; he told how he had discharged his pistol first into the air, and how he had been forced to fire the second time. _

"And even then," said he, "my bullet must have struck the earth and glanced upward, for I meant not to fire at my antagonist. But he fell— shot dead—and I, covered with shame, and bur- dened with sorrowful regret, fled from the place which had ceased to be a home for me." ' _ . _ _
Sir Jasper listened to the end, and then extended his hand. "My boy, I honour you. Let that suffice for the past. You say you had wished to join the army?' sir." " Do you wish it still t

"I do." "Then consider your wish gratified. I have in my possession two commissions, placed in my hands by officers in England who had got tired of the service. I. think I may claim that you held promise of a lieutenant's commission yesterday, and when the events of this day are known at the Bengal Presidency, I am mistaken if they do not deem you worthy of promotion, under which cir- cumatances I have a captain's commission open for you." " Sir Jasper—" "Pshaw I None of that. I am still the debtor."

" But, sir—" "If you get the full commission, my dear boy," again interrupted the baronet, "the service will be the gainer. So consider that as settled. If it comes to the expression of gratitude, I have as much of that material at heart as you have. Re- member—l have received my life at your hands. Don't forget it." Half an hour later Arthur stood leaning against one of the earronades, when Mary Wallace came up and stood by his side. She advanced confi- dently and frankly, and extended her hand with- out hesitation.

"Mr. Rainsford, I have no words with which to express the gratitude—the honour—aye, the rever- ence—which is due you. Little dreamed I, when my guardian gave you the trust, how nobly—how grandly—it was to be upheld." "My dear lady," said Arthur, "I should be false to myself were I to refuse your gratitude ; but you must remember that I was but one of many who did their whole duty truly and bravely." " Ah," responded Mary, with delicate chiding in her kindly tones, "I know what you did. My guardian has told me and Captain Harlow has told me. I know what spirit led our brave crew 'to victory. You will not deny me the privilege of ! believing them." "If you deem it a privilege, lady—..most assuredly not." _ .
"Thank you, Mr. Rainsford." And she took his hand again, as a sister might have done, and pressed it in the deep warmth of her grati- tude.

The rising moon but little on the wane, lighted up the beautiful face of the maiden as with a celes- tial halo, and the youth felt his heart thrill to its very core as he met the kindly, trustful gaze of those moistened eyes. There was a depth of gleaming in their dewy light that told of emotions far below the surface, and the waking smile that softened the lines of sorrow which the events of the day had drawn upon her harmonious features bespoke a con- fidence and esteem such as may be felt only where there is perfect trust. And then they talked of the battle, and, by deli- cate persuasion, Mary led her hero to tell of his own part in the work. At first he shrank from recounting the deeds which he had done, but as his spirit warmed in memory of the fray his tongue was loosened, and he gave to his attentive listener an account which none other could have given so well. The two commissions which Sir Jasper had re- ceived in England, from officers who had returned, on leave, from their regiments, and of which he was to dispose in India, had been transferred to him by the War Office so far in carte blanche that he was at liberty to dispose of them to whom he pleased, sub- ject only to the approval of the governor-general. So he forthwith invested Arthur with the commis- sion of lieutenant, to date from the day of the ship's leaving Bristol, at the same time giving assuranoe that tke_ raj* of captain sbould be his

upon their snivel in i_Talcutta, dating from the day of the battle with the pirates. His own personal influence, he felt, in conjunction with the blank commissions, fully warranted him in giving such assurance. The days passed on, and the ship entered the Indian Ocean. Arthur and Mary were much to- gether, and they were never at a loss for subjects upon which to converse. Despite his many scholarly short-comings while in college the youth had stored his quick and retentive mind with much valuable knowledge, and he was now able to instruct a willing pupil in many branches of polite and classic lore. What were the under-currents of feeling that moved the secret forces of those two natures it were not difficult to determine. Since the day when the sexes first learned that deepest and holiest of all human passions—the love which comes of an entire abnegation of self, and the mingling of two souls into one—it has always been the same, and must so continue while the heart of man throbs with human impulses. Two hearts free till now from the touch of the Erotic Archer, brought int° the warmth of gratitude beneath this sunshine of beauty and goodness and true bravery, with truth and honour and loyalty attending, have no escape from the common lot. At least Arthur Rainsford had not escaped. He had come to regard the beautiful being who blessed him with her smiles as the one angel of life whose ministrations of love had become necessary to his existence. He had not spoken this passion— he had not dared,—he felt that he was not yet in a situation to venture the bold avowal. In point of rank, if Lord Birchmear had east him entirely off, Mary was above him; and in point of wealth he was but a beggar in comparison. Not much en- couragement in these considerations. And yet he was not without hope. He was sure that his love was returned. There is a language of the soul, framed never into speech, which true love seldom, If ever, translates amiss; and if this language were to be trusted, then the youth had ample ground for his hopes. And, further than all this; Mary's guardian, knowing, as he must, if he had eyes to see, and a heart to understand, what were likely to be the consequences of the continued intimacy between his beautiful ward and the brave and handsome youth who had won his way to her confidence and esteem through the most tender and vulnerable portal of the female heart—Sir Jasper, knowing this, had not offered a remonstrance. He had not even hinted to his ward that she was in danger; nor had he signified to Arthur that he was trespas- sing. It was not impossible however, that the baronet, giving his young friend the credit of com- mon sense, conceived it entirely unlikely that one in his position should look with other than friendly feelings upon the heiress of one of the fairest manors in England. . .
But— Arthur did not borrow trouble. The sun shone too brightly, and the zephyrs were too soft, for the heralding of clouds. . . . .

Still, the time— e.ame when he began to regard the matter in a serious light. The ship had entered the Bay of Bengal, and in a very few days the voyage would be over. As the time of separation drew near our hero began to realise into what world of darkness he must be cast if this bright star of hope were to be blotted out from the heaven his existence. He now knew how deeply and how strongly he loved her. Did Mary loved him with a corresponding ardour?

Palmyras Point was passed, and on the following day they would enter the Hoogly. That evening Arthur and Mary stood together in the old place upon the lee side of the quarter-deck. The youth knew that she had not come accidentally. She had sought the place with the assurance that he would join her there. They spoke of the near approach of the termination of the voyage, of the pleasant associations that must give place to new and uncer- tain events, and of the promises therewith held out. After a pause they took up and reviewed a few of the more important episodes of the passage. Then followed another pause. The same spell seemed to hold them both in silence. When Arthur saw that his companion's eyes were cast down, and that a perceptible tremor shook her frame, he made sure that her feelings were conson- ant with his own.

"Mary," he said—he had called her so many times of late—" in a few short hours we shall leave this ship, and our ps.ths will lie apart." "How apart ?" she asked, looking up into his face. There was an eagerness in her expression which she could not restrain.
" You will go with your guardian, and I, if my commission be approved, must join my regi- ment."

"But, Arthur, Sir Jasper does not intend that you shall at once enter the service. He means that you shall be his companion, free from the trammels of military duty, until you shall have seen some• what of the country." "Sir Jasper is very kind, but he is incon- siderate."
" Inconsiderate ? He is not prone to act incon- siderately, Arthur." "And yet, my sweet lady, in this instance he forgets himself—or, I should say—he forgets— = 1"
"Forgets you, Arthur?" "Aye," responded the youth. "He forgets all but his generous wish to do me service; and in that forgetfulness he sees not how deeply he may wound me."

"Arthur, I do not comprehend." "Lady !—Mary !—I would hold back the words if I could; but they will out. I cannot hold them where they strive to burst my heart. To me, during the voyage that is now about to close, there has come a joy-beam that must leave my soul blank and dark indeed in its fading from my life. Already I am a slave to the blissful impulse, and my heart is captive for evermore. Were I the happy occupant of a position in which I could step side by side with Sir Jasper—were my prospects— But you know all I would say in that direction." "And,' interrupted Mary, in a tone of gentle reproof, "I know that you do my uncle injustice. His heart is true to the nobler instincts of his nature, and while you are true to the manhood that is in you, he will never bold himself above you —never 1, :

" Ah I dear lady! but were I to ask him for the one dearest gift within his power to bestow, were I to tell him that I already coveted the price- less treasure, and that further association would only render the refusal more bitter would he then, think you, bid me still bear him com- pany ?" Mary looked up with a shining light in her soft brown eyes, and though her voice trembled, yet there was no sign of hesitation. "I think my guardian would refuse you, per- emptorily, nothing which you might with propriety ask at his hands."-
"But," urged Arthur, borne on by an impulse which now swayed all his thoughts, "suppose I were to ask him to give to my life and to my love forever his own sweet ward 2"

Mary trembled violently, and yet she answered promptly: "He might ask you to wait until he could be assured that his ward's happiness would be secured by the event. Were he thus assured, lam very confident that he would refer you to the lady herself."

"Mary 1-0 I—lf I can, in the future, gain a place in the world—if I can establish my manhood upon a basis that shalt be firm and true—then— then—" "Then," said Mary, giving him both her hands, and looking up with a holy light in her dewy eyes, "I can love you no better than I love you now. My heart is all your own, Arthur; and if, in the time to come, you are as brave to save my peace and joy as you hase been in the time that is past to save my life—" The last words were whispered with her head pillowed upon her lover's bosom, and a flood of rapturous tears drowned the rest of the sentence. But to our hero hope was given, and he blessed Cod for the sacred boon. He forgot all the dark- ness of the years that were gone; he forgot all enmities and dangers that had threatened him— forgot everything but the one bright flood of pro- mise that had thus burst upon his life—and he felt in his heart the assurance of manly strength suffi- cient to bear him on to the deserving and the win- ning of the prize. Had some passing spirit,. in that blissful hour, whispered it into Arthur Rainsfoed's ear that a, simple sentence of only three or four words, spoken by an evil genius, might have been sufficient tio drive Mary Wallace from him in horror and dismay, he would have treated it as a wild and fanciful thing—a thing preposterous and impossible. And yet, many times, there had been a word upos the maiden's lips which, had it been spoken. wo- have given him a clue to the dreadful poWlailik

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Thursday last week. The Mayor (Councillor James Fairclongh) presided, and there were also present—Aldermen Harrison, Sutton, Wright, Balton, Hutchinson, and Greenall; Coun- cillors Shaw Green, Muir, Lee, Baird, Hepherd, Garner, Evans, Smethurst, Monks. Wilkinson, Woods, Bennett, Shillcock, Skelton, Hill, Beaman, Longton, and Roberts; Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), and S. Wilson (assistant town clerk).

div.head: LONG SERVICE POLICEMEN.
div.p: LONG SERVICE POLICEMEN.

In the minutes ot the Watch C.ntarnittee. it was reported that the Chief Constable had submitted the following return of the members of the police force entitled to superannuation :—Samuel Hunt, chief con- stable, who was appointed on 21st December, 1863 ; William Jameo,inspector, appointed 29'h July, 16t65 ; J. C. Spinks, inspector, 12th July, 1566; J. Chantler, sergeant, 14th April,ll.B7o. The minut,.s were adopted on the motion of the MAYOR.

div.head: FINANCE AND ESTATE COMMITTER,
div.p: FINANCE AND ESTATE COMMITTER,

Thiscommittee recorded that the sum ot £BO be voted to the borough auditors for their services in auditing the accounts of the Corporation for the year 1894-5. The committee had also resolved that the borough treasurer be authorised to take up the sum of £12,00 to replace loans called in on the reduction of the rate of interest ; and that the sinking fund to be providA for the repay- ment of the debt on the waterworks undertaking be es- tablished on the principle of redemption by equal yearly instalments of principal and interest. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Coun- cillor SH&W GREEN. STREET INFECI cEMENT AND LIGHTING 'COMMITTEE .—NEW

div.head: B UI LDINGS.
div.p: B UI LDINGS.

This committee recorded that the following buildings. &c., he approved ::—Amended plan of 19 houses eff Marshhouse-lane, for Mr. Joseph Matthews (condition- ally) ; shop at the corner of Howley-lane and Ezerton- strer.t, for Mr. Thomas Davies ; cellar to shop, No. 90, linutsford.road, for Mr. William Bolton. 12 houses in Miller-street. for Mr. Richard Miller ; 18 cottages in Forster-st.' .for Mr. Peter Rigby; U 4 cottages in Forster- street, for Mr. Thomas Worsley; :8 houses in Dadley-st., for Mr. John Appleton ; new premises in florsemarket- at., for W. P. and W. Skelton, Limited. Alderman Strreimir moved, and Alderman Waioar seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Councillor BENNETT referred to the plans for 19 houses in Marshhowe-lane and asked what was meant by the word "conditionally." He also suggested that now they had plans foir new premises for Messrs. Skelton's before them it would be a good oppertunity to make alterations to the shop at the corner of Lyme-st., which would be suitable to the Corporation and the other parties interested. . .

Alderman SUTTON, in reply, said the c,mditions they had imposed in connection with the houses in Marsh- house-lane was that a piece of land at the back should be kept an open space for all tim.. As to the shop in Horsernarket-st. the Corporation could still deal with that at any future time.
'Fhe minutes were confirmed. TUE HEALTH COMMITTEE.-.-TITE ABATTOIR, AND SMALL-PDX
HOSPITAL.

The minutes of the committee contained the rasoln- tions as to a public abattoir and a small-pox hospital which we published last week .The cmimittee had also re- solved that permission be granted to Mr. Arthur Cawley to establish the trade of glue-making on premises in Lythgoes-lane. Alderman SUTTON moved the confirmation of the minutes. As to the iproposed small-pox hospital the committee had for some time past endeavoured to find a suitable plan in the neighbourhood for a hospital, but they had been perfectly °cable to do so. They had, therefore come to the conclusion that they should utilise for the purpose the land near Houghton Green which belonged to the Corporation. They had at all events instxucted the Medical Officer and Borough Sorveyor to give a report and if their report was satisfactory they should ask the permission of the Council to use the place as a site, and when they had made their arrangements they would submit to the other authorities who were denirous of joining them in the hospital the terms they felt disposed to grar.t them. As to the proposed abattoir the resolution they had passed simply expressed an opinion by the committee. Anything further that they might decide upon would be submitted to the Council. Councillor Romurrs seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor SICHIP.ON said he should like it to be dis tinctly understood that the matter would be again sub- mitted to the Council before the Committee proceeded to erect a abattoir. , Alderman SurTon said that was so. . . .

'COUIIeinOrSEIAW GREEN said there arm a st itement in the report that the amount coming in from an abattoir would be sufficient to pay for the outlay, but he was told that the number of animals given as being slaughtereu in Warrington was in excess of the real number so slaughtered. He hoped that the figures given would be accurate. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Woons remarked that it was not compul- sory for every butcher to slaughter animals in Warring- ton. It was quite on the car is that if the a r ran gernents did not suit the butchers they might slaughter just out- side the boundary. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SANITARY WORKS COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE SANITARY WORKS COMMITTEE.

The Sanitary Works Committee had passed the fol- lowing resolutions: —That tho Cmtirmnto, Do mt man and Mr. Deas be appointed to attend the Annual Congress of the British Institute cf Public ['eolith, to be held in Bull on the Bth to 13th August ; and that Mr. 1 William Floughton and Mr. Charles Rigby beappointed Agent § to the Corporation for the sale of concentrated manure. . _
The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Coun- cillor MONK* seconded by Councillor BEAMAN.
PAVING AND SEWERAGI3 COMMITTEE. -THE PROYOSED
CORPORATION WEIARP.

, This committee recommended the following tenders I for acceptance ; of Messrs. Henry Wadsworth and Son to supply a street sanding machine a. £45; of Mr. Joseph S. Garlamd to simply patent revolting disc street watering machine at £56, and a patent sanitary tumbler cart at £29; of Messrs. Sayce and Randlo to construct a wharf wall at Howley for the sum of £704 18s. Bd., and for excavating ground at 23. per cubic yard ; and of Messrs. Jones and Company to supply 500 square yards of 2in. concrete flags at 33.11 d. per square yard and the tender of Messrs. Crombie and Son, of Middlesborough tnsupply 500 square yards at 3s. Bd. per square yard. They also recommended that in the event of any person being allowed to withdraw any tender for works after such tender has been accepted he be debarred from ten- dering for other works for 12 months afterwards. Alderman WRIGHT in proposing the minutes of this committee said that they intended to erect a permanent wharf beside their stone yard opposite the river side at a cost of £704 Mi. Bd. It would be a permanent struc- ture and he believed it would save the Corporation not less than £lOO or £l2O per annum. Alderman fluvormsoN seconded the minutes, Councillor SIIILLCOCK called the attention of the Chair- man to the very bad state of the street under the Central Station. Water was constantly running across the footpath, and it was almost impassible in wet weather. Councillor HILL called attention to thestate of Orford. street which he said was in the centre of the town, hut was a disgrace to Warrington, in fact it was the worst street in Warrington. _ . _ . . .

Councillor SKELTON Raid that he noticed that on the minutes there was a further recommendation for the excavating of ground at 2s. per cubic yard, at the wharf. He wished to know what that would cost. Councillor MONKS would like to know whether the tender in question was the only tender received by the committee, and whether it was the lowest. His idea was that it was a very big sum for such a wharf. This wharf would be much more costly than other whsrves which had been built. Alderman WRIGHT said that the footpath under the Central Station had received the . attention of the Com- mittee. Be had heard nothing about Orford-street prev- iously, but it would have the attention of the committee. With regard to the excavating in the wharf, he had been informed by the borough surveyer that the expenses would be nil. In reply to Councillor Monks he would say that there were other tenders, and the one accepted waP the lowest. The minutes were passed unanimously. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. The minutes a this committee wee proposed by Councillor SHAW GREEN who said that as it was well- known the senior school attendance officer had resigned. A considerable number of applications had been made for the vacant office and they would be considered at the next meetina. Councillor SLIILLCOCK seconded the minutes which were passed unanimously. MUSEUM, ETC., COMMITTEE.—INCREASE OF BORROWERS. The committee reported the following gifts, for which the thanks of the committee were ordered to he sent the donors :—British shells, 27 specimens, Ophiealeit.e pebbles. from lona, from Mr. W. H. Fleathcote ; speci- mens (19) to illustrate processes of metal work,frsin T. Fletcher; honks for the blind, 9 vols., fro.n Mr. %V. Grimshaw ; Bible in Maori, from Mr. H. Davies. They also reported a very large increase in the number of books lent during the past five years. Councillor ROBERTS, in moving the minutes, said that he had no doubt the Council would be gratified by noting the enormous increase in the distribution of books in the lending department during the last five years. The increase was 300 per cent. ahnost,which was a very good testimony tm the popularity of that valuable institution, the free library. Councillor MONKS seconded, and the minutes were passed unanimously. , CEMETERY COMMITTEE.—IMPROVED CONDITION OF THE

CEMETERY. The report of the Registrar to this committee stated that the interments for the past four weeks were— adults, 20 ; minors, 24 ; stillborn and premature, 8 ; corresponding period last year—adults, 38 ; minors, 44; stillborn and premature, 11. The receipts for the past four weeks were £43 121. 2d. ; corresponding period last year, £77 103. Bd.

Alrierman Eleartisox proposed the minutes and said that it would repay anyone to go to the cemetery si it was in an excellent condition, and it must be pleasing to see that the graves were so well kept. Councillor Elm, seconded. Alderman WRIGHT also expresiiied his plesure thlt the cemetery was so much improved. Ile had had on-, to visit the cemetery more frequently of late an, i tn was pleased with its • condition, and the chairman of the committee was to be congra'iulated upon the result. The minutes were passed unanimously. TOWN FULL, RTC., COMMITTEE. .

The report ofthe batitkepper to the committee stated the income from the baths for the past eight weeks was £134. 153. 2i.. and for the corresponding period last year was £2OO 7s. Alderman BOLTON proposed the Committee's minutes.

Alderman GREENALL seconded. After a few observations by Councillors R. T. FAIR- CLOUGH and SMETHURST, with reference to the state of the Town Hall building, the minutes were passed unani- mously. MARKETS COMMITTEE.—TNE SALES IF THE MARKET. TrUS Committee reported that the total income from all sources for the past four weeks was £3690;. 81. ; cor- respondin. period last year, £327 9s. 51. ; increase, £4l 11i. 3d. They also recommended that the town clerk issue the following notice :—" Notice is hereby given that the wholesale vegetable market in Queen-st., will, on and after the 3rd day of August next, be opened at 5 o'clock in the morning on the usual market days, and be closed at 10 o'clock in the morning on such day " ; and also that the horse and cattle fairs be no longer held in the public streets. Allerman GREENALL proposed, and Alderman FILT• cumsox seconded the minutes. . .

~„ Councillor SKELTON asked whether there had been any alternative scheme to suggest before carrying out the re- solution with reference to the cattle fairs. Councillor SMETHURST said that the farmers ought not to be turned out of the market so early as ten o'clock. If the notice the Committee proposed were enforced, farmers would often have to take their stuff away again. Ile knew of several farmers who were going to St. Helens and would not come near the Warrington market at all.

Alderman WRIGHT said that he had been appealed to by respectable farmers who said that they would be per- fectly satisfied if the time was extended until eleven o'clock. Alderman SUTTON also stated that it was a great hard- ship to the farmers to have to go out of the market 80 early as ten o'clock. Alderman HUTCHINSON, as a tivrnber of the Commit- tee, said that when the subject was discussed, the Com- mittee were divided as to whether the time should be ten or eleven o'clock, and those in favour of ten were in the majority. It was understood that, if on a trial, ten o'clock was not a favourable time for closing, the Com- mittee would agree to alter it to eleven o'clock. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH wanted to know if it was likely that a pig market would be opened in Warrington again. Alderman GREENALL said that he was not in a position to make any statement as to the pig market. With re- gard to the notice to which reference had been made by various members of the Council, he believed it had been brought about by the request of certain farmers them- selves. It was impossible to please everybody, and they had all kinds and &additions of men in that market. It had been thought by the majority of the Committee that it was advisable to try the notice, and if it was found not to work well, they would try to alter it. Let the farmers go to St. Helens if they wished. They would not get better treatment there, as he had found by in- quiry from tbe officials in that place. To use a Lanca- shire phrase, they were trying to " bullyrag " the Corporation by saying that they could get cheaper rotes at St. Helens, and they told those in St Helens that they could get cheaper rates in Warrington. As regarded the question of the cattle fair, he was not in a position to give any details. Councillor SHELTON rose to propose an amendment to the minutes, but as the Chairman of the committee had replied, he was ruled out of order, and the minutes were then passed.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 24 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 24 1895.

they wanted to reduce the expenses. Mr. Ross, the pre- sent engineer, had £4OO a year, a house and other etcetras,and they would make a saving upon that by the proposed arrangement. Mr. Deas had all the know- ledge requisite for a water engineer at his finger ends, and he (Mr. Green) was told that Mr. Dees hod brought out of something like chaos at Longford a well-arranged department. (Hear, hear.) Another point was that in the water department they required all the income they could get to enable them to pay their sinking fund and interest. If they could obtain suitable service for some- thing like £2OO or £250 a year they would be saving a considerable sum of money. Alderman GREEN&LL thought the Water Committee had shown great weakness as they ought to have ad- vertistad. If Mr. Dees undertook that,would be give up his private business ? His vote would depend on the answer to that question. Councillor HEPHERD moved an amendmeut that the minute referring to the appointment of water engineer be referred loam The question with him was whether I Mr. Dees was fully qualified as a water engineer ? He objected to a dual control in the affairs of the Corpora- tion, and he thought that the saving that would be effected by the proposed arrangement would only be £5Ol year. Alderman WRIGHT seconded the amendment, and said I that an enormous property like the waterworks justified ' the appointment of one man to look after It, He also understood that Mr. Dees had got some private business of his own under the name of Beaman and Dees or Dees and Beaman which must take up Some of his time. Alderman SUTTON supported the minutes of the Com- mittee. He argued that there would boa saving ef £3OO by the proposed arrangement. Councillor ROBERTS supported the minutes of the Com- mittee. It had, he said, been quite refreshing that even- ing to find that Councillor Hepherd had bten able to give some reasons for what he did. (Laughter.) But the argument that because the water undertaking repre- sented a capital of £277,000 it required the entire services of an engineer to look after it was utterly beside the question, That large sum represented the value of the monopoly to supply Warrington with water and not merely the machinery, and it could not therefore, be compared with the capital of some other undertakings. As to the objections to dual control, he pointed out that there were a number of cases in this country where the gas and water engineers were the same. It was not a separate -nan for each undertaking that was wanted but a man capable of management and with the necessary knowlede.e of administration and of machinery. (Hear, hear.) The water works undertaking was in a most critical condition. They were rapidly reaching the time when their capital repayment would have to commence and their present income would not be equal to the de- mand of capital and interest, The very last thing that any of them would like to see would be the water under- taking becoming a charge upon the rates. (Hear, hear.) Yet, that was staring them in the face for two reasons. The first was that, as he had said, the time before the repayments commenced was rapidly expiring, and in the second place because they had lost during the last two years customers to a very large amount and those cus- tomers would have to be made up for in some ether way. ' With proper management and with a capable man,—a man who will attract customers rather than repel them the derived result,so far at least as the increase of custom was concerned, would be brought about. It would be little short of madness if when they had the opportunity of putting a thoroughly capable man in the position and saving between £3OO and £4OO a year, which was nearly half the amount of their deficit, they did not take the opportunity. (Hear, hear). Alderman Hammon said that as he did not know Mr Deas,he might be credited with speaking impartially. He never had greater pleasure than he had that night in voting for the resolution of the Water Committee.(Uear, hear.) From what he had read of Mr. Deas, he was the very man for the position. With regard to his holding a dual position, they knew many competent men in this country holding dual positions. Lord Salisbury, if he might allude to 'politics—(laugnter)—held a dual posi- tion—(hear, hear)—Mr. Balfour held a dual position, and they knew that in the last ministry there were posi- tions of a dual character,and vet were not prejudicial in any way to the public interest. Therefore when they had an opportunity and opening for a man—he was go- ing to say a genius,and if they were to judge fairly what Mr. Deas had accomplished since he cdrne to Warrington rthey could almost put him under the category of a genius—they should take advantage of it,and he did not think they ran any risk at all. If they found that.con- trary to their expectations Mr. Dees was incapable of managing the business, they could make short work of it, and he did not think that Mr. Dees would feel that they had acted unjustly. He therefore felt that he had no hesitation whatever in supporting the minutes of the committee. (Hear, hear.) Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said that he had taken the troulele to see some of the directors of the late Water Works Company to get their advice upon the subject. Ile bad great respect tor Mr. Dees and every confidence in him, but he was told by the directors of the late com- pany that a great deal depended upon the distribution of the water. That was a serious matter and they ought to have some one with a technical knowledge of the dis- tribution of the water. He did not know that Mr. Dees had that knowledge, but lie would not like to vote against him. He could not vote for him and he there- fore declined to vote at all. Councillor MONKS, as chairman of the Sanitary Works Committee, said that he would like to say that the pro- posed arrangement had not come before the Council at the request of the Committee, nor was it as the result of any action taken by the Committee, nor so far as he knew of any individual member of the Committee. It had been entirely at the initiative of the Water Commit- tee. They had considered the proposal and the Sanitary Works Committee were unanimously of opinion that they could arrange so that Mr. Deas could have a sufficient amount of time to devote to the Water Works Commit- tee's business. They considered that he was wasting his time and abilities at Longford. Mr. Deas was at present in sole charge at Longford, and by not having a man as a foreman,they were entirely in Mr. Deas' hands. If , he left for any reason, there was no one being trained in view of conducting that business. They were entirely , unprepared with a successor. It was not desirable to be dependent upon one man. By the proposed arrange- ment, he contended that there would be an immediate saving of £9O per annum. Alderman Greenall had said something about private practice. but he (Councillor Monks), could inform the Council, that since 2r. Dees I had been at Longford, he had' done no private work whatever. He had a brother in Warrington, who was in charge of the Company which had been mentioned. He was very similar in appearance, and they were liable to be mistaken for each ether. Mr. Dees was dependent upon his salary. Councillor BRAMAN also emphatically repudiated the report that Mr. Deas had any private business. 'Phe amendment was then put to the vote, and for it there voted, Aldermen Wright and Hutchinson, and Councillors Skelton, Hill, and HPpherd, 5; against the M iyor, Aldermen Greenall,Harrison,Sutton, and Bolton, and Councillors Roberts, Shaw Green, Bennett, Shill- cock, Lee, Evans, Lengton, Wilkinson, Garner, Beaman, Baird, and monks, 17.
_ The amendment was therefore lost, and the minutes were then carried.
GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.-TRE WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET. _

The committee recommended that the letter from Messrs. W. A. Bishop and Co. set out on the proceedings of the Rivers Comtnittee having been read, it was resolved that the Rivers Committee be requested to con- fer with the Paving and Sewerage Committee, and with I their concurrence to re-opect negotiations with Messrs. Bishop and Co. with a view to their taking a lease of a portion of the river frontage of the Howley stone yard for the purposes of a wharf ; also that Mr. Councillor R. T. Fairclough be appointed to represent the Corporation on the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissibn for the term of three years ; also that the Mayor, Alderman Blacichurst, and Councillor Monks be appointed a special committee to negotiate and report upon the purchase of property for the widening of Bridge-street. The MAYOR proposed, and Alderman GREENALL seconded the minutes.

div.head: GAS COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS COMMITTEE.

This Cimmittee recommended the following tenders for acceptance; Cross, Tetley and Company Limited, 7,000 tons of coal; Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company Limited, 10,000 tons of slack ; Abram Coal and Cannel Company Limited. 3,000 tons of slack; Mr. E. Aukland,junior,to supply 182 dressed longridge stones at £ssBs. 101. ; also that an order for £5,195 23. 51. be made,and the amount be forwarded to the borough trea- surer. They reported that the average illuminating power of the gas for the past six weeks was equal to 18.50 candles at both works. They also recommended that the following scale of wages be adopted ; to take effect from the 31st March,lB96 :—E. J. Smith, preseet salary, £llO, maximum. £l5O, annual increase £8 10s. ; to take effect from the 31st March, 1895, R. Rind, !present salary £65, maxi- mum, £l3O, annual increase, £5 4s. ; A. Wood present salary, £52, maximum, £l3O, annual increase, £5 45. ; Junior Clerk, present salary, commence at 6s. per week,maximum, £lo4,annual increase £5 4s. ; at 20 years of age the latter to be raised to 203. per week ; also that 500 tons of cannel be purchased from the Padeswood Cannel and Coal Company Limited. Councillor R. T. FAIRCIOUGH proposed the minutes and said that the committee did not wish to trouble the Council with increases of salaries being constantly brought before them, and they had adopted a scale of salaries to the clerks of the department so that they should know what they would got. . . .

Councillor FlEynnan seconded the minutes. Alderman BOLTON thought that the committee were trying to eyad the standing orders whereby increases in salaries of £2 per week and upwards should come before the Council.

Cooncillor SHAW GREEN said that the question ought to have been brought uo in February. which was the customary time for discussing the questions of salaries. He did net disapprove of the principle involved, but ob- jected to the matter being brought forward at the present time. Alderman HARRISON wouldlike to ask the Chairman of the committee a question with reference to the imposi- tion of meter rents upon the consumers. If ever there was an iniquity invented, he believed it was that. He wished to ask if there was any probability of the com- mittee taking any action in the matter with a view to reducing or abolishing that imposition. They were doing so in other towns and Warrington could not do better than follow the example. It was an iniquitous thing to charge for the rent of the meter.

Councillor HEPHERD . We kept them in order. Councillor ROBERTS contended that it was not fair that the officials of the gas department alone should escape the supervision and criticism of the Council in regard to their salaries. He wig in favour of the princi- ple, but he would like it applied all round. After some further discussion, Councillor R. T. FAIR- CLOTIGH said that he would withdraw the miautes with reference to the salary of Mr.E. J. Smith, which was the only one the Council could control.
The minutes were then passed unanimously. THE RIVERS COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this Committee contained a letter from Councillor Greening in which that gentleman expressed a wish to resign his positioia as a member of the Rivers Committee "to mark his strong disapproval of the action of the Council at its last meeting" with reference to the Committee's minutes. div.head: DETECTIVE ABILITY.
div.p: DETECTIVE ABILITY.

Detective work, method, and experience proves, with- out a doubt, most interesting to the general reader. There is something especially exciting and fascinating in having mirrored the little, seeming unimportant clues which an astute and clever detective will follow to a successful issue. In former days one's imagination was roused by dressing our detectives in rapidly-changing disguises, which were supposed to aid him in unravelling the puzzle ; latterly etsr ablest detectives have adopted a different basis, and rely more upon qualification,ability, and perspicacity to save them from embarrassing or dangerous positions. We think the interest attached to these experiences revolves upon the constant surprises in store for one who is a close observer and makes an intelligent use of the simplest signs or symptoms bear- ing upon the case. The same interest is manifest in matters of health. There are many signs and symptoms which, if accurately read, would warn us of approach- ing ailments in time to ward them off. If, on the other hand, disease fastens upon us quickly—almost without warning—then the careful observer may perhaps call to mind what Mr. George H. Bowden of 21, Beaumont Street, Cowpen Quay, Blyth. did under similar circum- stances, and he guided by this experience, which will en- sure an equally satisfactory result. lie writes : "Three years ago my health suddenly broke down. I tried several local doctors before they told me what my complaint was. At last one of them told me it was Bright's dis- ease of the kidneys, and said there was no cure for me. I at last decided to go to the Infirmary; their diagnosis was the same, having found albumen, blood, and casts in my water. After eight weeks in bed, on a milk diet, I returned home, no better, but much weaker than when I went, and nothing before me but death. My wife then persuaded me to try Warner's Safe Cure. I had but little faith, but from the first bottle I found relief, and a few weeks' perseverance completed my cure,feel as well as ever I did in my life, thanks to this mar- vellous remedy, which I never fail to recommendandlnew two anyone showing signs of kidney disease."

div.head: PUELIC-HOLISE APPEALS.
div.p: PUELIC-HOLISE APPEALS.

Alderman BOLTON appealed on the ground that the assessment on his public-house in Mersey-street was too high. He appealed to the committee to value the house independent of imperial taxation.—Mr. William Hough- ton said that they could not value it at less that the imperial taxation.—A long argument ensued between Mr. Bolton and the committee in which the former ac- cused the latter of unfairness and Mr. Bolton was then asked to retire while the Committee considered the case. When Mr. Bolton again entered the room, the Chairman said that the committee had given the case very careful consideration, and nothing that would be said had shown any reason why the assessment should be reduced 'The committee were influeneed in their assessment by more considerations than Mr. Bolton seemed to think of, and they had come to the conclusion that he was fairly assessed.—Mr. Bolton appealed against the assessmedt of the beer-house at Pitt-street but this appeal was also dismissed.—Mr. Bolton said that he was over. assessed, but the Clerk imformed him that the committee were obliged to assess public-houses at not less than the imperial taxation, otherwise it would be unfair to the other ratepayers. If Mr. Bolton were under assessed, the money would have still to be found to pay the county rate, and thus the other ratepayers would have to pay what was short,which was obviously unfair. Mr. Bolton ought to appeal against the imperial tax. I Mr. Berry, the landlord of the Leigh Arms, Newton, I appealed for the reduction of the assessment upon his house. He said that he had taken the advice of the committee at their last meeting when he had appealed, and had had his imperial tax reduced ,and he now applied for his assessment to be reduced. The application was granted.

div.head: IRON AND STEEL INSTITUTE.
div.p: IRON AND STEEL INSTITUTE.

There was a large attendance of members at the open- ing meeting of the Iron and Steel Institute, at Birming- ham on Tuesday. Sir David Dale presided, and papers were read dealing chiefly with the present condition of the iron and steel industries of South Staffordshire and the mineral resources of the district.—M. Bonehill, of Marchienne au Pont, Belgium, described the satisfactory results that had attended experiments in Belgium for the direct puddling of iron from the blast furnaces. It oc- curred to him, he said, that it would bl advantageous to collect the metal tapped from the blast furnace in a reservoir, where it could he maintained in a fluid state, and from which it could subsequently be transferred to the puddling furnace. The puddling furnace was on the Siemens system, and was heated by four producers, be- neath which were placed the regenerators. These fur- naces gave better results when applied to the direct pro- cess than when the iron to be puddled was charged in the form of pigs. The reason for that was obvious. There was never any cooling of the gas, which was al- ways in contact with metal at a high temperatere consequently the regenerators did not become cooled, and toe air for combustion always entered at the highest temperature. The metal flowed directly from the blast furnace into the reservoir, and that resulted in an im- portant saving of labour, as the pig moulders, weighers, and wheelers were dispensed with. It resulted in the obviation of accidents that occurred when casting the pigs, and as the melted metal was taken born the reservoir by the puddiers- themselves a further economy of labour was obtained. The fuel used amounted to 20 per cent., whilst in the ordinary furnace it ranged froth 100 per cent. upwards. The loss of metal was reduced to the least amount prac- tically possible, and the charge, instead of remaining an hour and a half in the furnace, stayed there less than an I hour. He calculated that the saving per ton of puddled I iron was 11,788 i. —roughly spealting,24. in labour,B a. 3d. I in fuel, and 3s. Bd, in waste—and claimed that the pro- duct was refined better, was very uniform, and was stronger than by the ordinary process.—On this paper there was some discussion.—Sir Benjamin Hingley said that if all M. Bonehill claimed was true it would work a revolution in puddling within the next few years.— Professor Turner, Birmingham, said the process of which the paper spoke might be suitable to the Spanish and Belgian works, but he was not sanguine that it could be applied to many of the furnaces of South Staffordshire. —Mr. Jeremiah Head, Middlesbrouf,,h,said that although they could not endorse all that was in the paper there was much that they could learn from it, and they were grateful to M. Bonahill.—Replying in French to a vote of thanks, M. Bsnehill regretted that although his grandfather came from Bilston he was unable to speak the English tongue.—The last paper of the morning was I one on the ironworks of South Russia, written by Mr. I George Kamensky, of St. Petersburg, in which he showed what had been done and what is being done by Russian and foreign capital to makelSouthern Russia one of the most important future centres of the iron trade in the world.—ln the evening the Mayor of Birmingham gave a reception.

The inaugural lecture of a series of ten lectures on" Varied Occupations" for the lower standards in schools, was delivered at Holy Trinity Schools on Tuesday night. VV. THE LEAGUE OF THE CROSS.

On Sunday evening the usual weekly meeting of the League of the Cross,was held in the League Hall Bewsey-at., at 830 p.m. In the temporary absence of the President. Mr. John Mullins, Mr. John Dal- ton, vice-president, opened the proceedings with an address on the evils of intemperance. Ile dwelt at length on the evils, evidence of which was from day to day appearing in the Press of the country The most appalling outrages were, be said, perpe- trated whilst under the baleful influence of this insidious devil drink. He gave his experiences in the homes of the poor in Liverpool, where, he said, you will find large,commodious, almost palatial gin palaces, erected in the midst of poverty stricken dwellings, the usual surroundings of such places, being squallor, filth and crime, accentuated to a 1 fearful degree by the most horrible outrages against Society and against the laws of the Supreme Being. We had in our midst, notwithstanding our boasted ' nineteenth century civilisation, a people who are absolutely ind.fferent about God, their salvation, their best interests, and the best interests of their families, were all sacrificed to this great Moloch drink. But the victims sacrificed to the deity of the Ammonites, sank into insignificance when compared with the victims sacrificed on the altar of Bacchus. He then gave some moving pictures of home life amongst the poor of Liverpool. He concluded with a forcible appeal to the members of the League, to bestir themselves and never to miss an opportunity of bringing men there on a Sunday night to hear the addresses and take the total abstinence pledge. Mr Mullins then addressed the meeting,and announced that on Sunday next the members of the Council and visitors wouli make a house to house visita- tion through all the wards in the town, and endea- vour to enlist all Catholics into the League. The total abstinence pledge was administered to thir- teen men by the Rev. Father Craven, 0.5.8.
