div.head: MASSACRE OF MISSIONARIES
div.p: THE MASSACRE OF MISSIONARIES
IN CIIINA.

Wycliffe Congregational Church was largely attended on Sunday night,when the pastor, the Rev. John Yonge, delivered a special sermon on the subject "The Mass- acre of Christian Miseionaries in China," and took as his text the 201 i verse of the 74th Psalm. "The dark places of the earth ar full e f the habitations of cruelty." This sentence, the rev. gentlemin oescribed as an apt des- cription of what has ever been the condition of heathen- dom. The heathen world was dark with terrible ignor- ance, which was often the parent of horrible cruelty. Of course it was true that even in civilized and Christian countries like our own, cruel and infamous deeds wer enacted, in which humanity was depraved below., the nature of savage beasts. But such deeds were excep- tional, and were visited at once by swift condemnation and adequate penalty. In heathendom, however, cruelty was native and continual, and often rampant. Atroci- ous crimes were committed even in the very name of religion ; but these cruelties sprung from the dense ignorance of heathenism. Could the light of the gremel penetrate the kingdoms held in this thraldom of dark- ness the days of cruelty weuld end. The fact of cruelty reigaing among heathens was, therefore, a powerful reason for the persistent continuance of mis- sionary enterprise, rather than for its abandonment. Seeing that the heathens often deemed it religious to be cruel, it was not surprising that they should now and again break forth in barbarous cruelty against those who sought to convert them. They hael done so frequently, believing they were thus defending their religion, and consequently the true missionary had opened up fielda of enterprise with his life in his hands. In recent years, however, the work of the missions had proceeded so quietly that it was beginning to be thought that the day of missionary peril had passed away ; but within the past few days the whole Christian world had had a rude awakenine, and once again the roll of martyrs for the faith of Christ had received a considerable accession. At an early hour on the morning of the Ist August, a. riot had broken out at the station of the Churce Mis- sionary at Whasang, near Kucheng, in China. The houses of the premises were set on fire, and ten persons killed, while several more were wounded. The murders were committed by a band of about 50 men, belonging to a society known as " the vegetarians." Naturally it had created the greatest alarm among European resi- dents in China, and had filled the friends of Missions in England and America with serious and painful anxiety. To us at home the event had come with startling sud- denness, but from very recent correspondence, an out- break had been feared for some time. The crime itself, however, had been accomplished in an entirely unlooked for moment, and with all possible savagery. The ;rev.. gentleman proceeded to enter into a detailed account of the experiences of Miss Hartford, the American lady, who very narrowly escaped death. He then remarked that the deepest sympathy would go forth to the friends ef the murdered missionaries, and to the parents, full of agony in such disastrous bereavement. But notwithstanding these terrible proceedings, the stricken mourners were lifting up their sorrowing hearts with Christian hope, and were not begrudging the costly sacrifice they bad been called upon to endure. The missionary band were not faltering or fainting, but on the contrary were de- claring their unfaltering adhesion to the enterprise,and were eagerly pressing forward to fill the places of the This noble bearing of the bereaved, and of the stricken missionary contingent, commended them most powerfully to the sympathy, admiration, and confidence of all the Churches. In missionary circles in America and this country, the question had been earnestly con- sidered and discussed as to what should be the mission- ary attitude in the present crisis. At a special meeting hl London on the previous Monday, the Eastern com- mittee of the London Missionary Society had debated the two main questions "Should any advices be sent out to China instructing the missionaries to retire for the present from those stations likely to be affected by the recent riots ? "and secondly " Should 'the mission- aries, whose departure from this country for China had been timed for autumn be delayed until the issue of events was made clear ? " Both these questions were after a long and careful discussion taken part in by three China missionaries,and answered in the negative,it being fully believed that the prompt and firm interven- tion of the British and American Government would prevent any further spread ef these terrible events. Other considerations had lead the committee to adept this course. The upshot of this committee meeting was, that the district committees in China were given dis- cretionary powers to act as they thought fit ; and that no change should be made respecting the prospective de- parture of Chinese missionaries this autumn.

It was noteworthy that the missionaries in China and also the foreign consuls and customs officials believed that the Chinese Government had been behind all at- tempts to molest and terrorize the foreigner. The Govern- ment was not anti-missionary but anti-foreign and their aim was to keep the foreigner, whether merchant or missionary, out of China. The Council of the Church Missionary Association passed a resolution the other day placing on record their unfaltering belief that no disasters, however great, should be allowed to interfere with the prosecution of the purpose for which the society existed. No other determination could have been consistent with the divine commission—to preach the Gospel to the world. If in the past the heralds of the Cross had desisted when met with opposition and persecution, how far different would have been the Christendom of to day ! Christian- ity had spread in spite of opposition. Over and over again had the old saying been verified " The blood of the martyrs,is the seed of the Church." The rev.gentleman then dealt with the hostile criticism of foreign missions and especially those in China. He quoted letters on the subject to prominent journals and denounced the criticisms as fallacious and their state- ments untrue,adding in answer to one that no Christian missions, even in China are faillres. For long, China was fast closed against Christianity but in 1842 and again in 1860 treaties were made in China which led to certain posts being opened and from 1842 to 1888 the missions prospered greatly. In the latter year there were 1,000 missionaries with 32,000 communicants, and the progress the rev, gentleman believed was con- tinued.

The preacher then dealt at length with the perils and difficulcies which beset the way of ths missionaries in China owing to the intense ignorance of the people, and he concluded by saying that no sacrifice was two pre- cious for Jesus, and that the martyrs of Kucheng called upon the Christian Church of every name, and in every land, to win China and the world for Christ,

SATURDAY, AUGUST 24, 1895.
ALTHOUGH the present Parliamen Tory Policy. is still very young there are already

significant indications of the line on which Tory policy will be developed. Every- one was familiar with the promises upon whish Unionist candidates fought and won the elections. In Warrington, for instance, what were the measures which were dangled before the electors in bold type, and enlarged upon at the Tory meet- ings? Mr. ROBERT PIERTOINT in his address told us that, in domestic affairs, we might under a Unionist Government look forward to "much- needed legislation in the direction of poor-law reform, old age pensions, cheap and easy transfer of land, restriction of foreign pauper immigration and the importation of poison-made goods; an amendment of the Employers' Liability Act, int- provetnent of the dwellings of the poor, facilities for workingmen to purchase their own dwellings, and many other measures of a domestic nature calculated to benefit the artisan class and the corn- ' 'nullity generally." This, with local variations to suit the tastes of different constituencies, was the general programme upon which not only Mr. Pinarorrir but nearly all the other Unionist candidates fought the election, and upon this programme as a whole the election ' was won. But the contest was barely over before certain Tory newspapers and some of the more candid Tory speakers began to minimise and even to deride several of the items of the programme which had done its Work as a nbsit" for the elec- tors. Measures which are "calculated, to benefit the artisan class aid the community generally are not the sort which ordinary Tories care much about. These therefore have already been allowed to drop into the background; they are scarcely ever mentioned now, but in their place another subject which is not even mentioned in Mr. PIER- POINT'S address has been rushed to the front with suspicious unanimity. This subject to which the Tory majority is being called upon to devote itself I first and foremost is euphemistically described as the "relief of agriculture." That is a very attrac- tive phrase. Agriculture is still, in spite of the gieat developments of manufacture and commerce the most important of British industries, and if it needs relief and can be relieved there can be no question that the relief should be given as speedily as possible. ;, But when an

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held at Dutton Work. house on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. J. Mclntyre, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present : Messrs. Joseph Knowles, Joseph Stokes, Thomas Lewis, T. Wright, E. Aaron, J. Spruce, J. L. Jones, C. Boylance, T. Baxter, C.C., T. Darlington, C. W. Davenport, S. Woodward, J. Brandreth, J. Derbyshire. W. Bradford, H. E. Heywood, H. Talbot, J P., and Dr. Adams (medical officer), Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), Messrs. Diegle and Swinton (surveyors), Mr. Farrington (nuisance inspector).

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICERSHIP.
div.p: THE MEDICAL OFFICERSHIP.

A letter from the Local Government Board was read, sanctioning the appointment of Dr. Mama as medical officer of health for the Rural District of Runcorn from the 26th March, 1895, to the 25th March, 1896, at a salary of £l2O per annum. The letter stated that the Board did not now think it necessary to impose any restrictions as regarded the period for which medical officers of health or inspectors of nuisances should be appointed, when the arrangements proposed were such as appeared to the Board to be satisfactory and if the Council should think it desirable to suhmit a proposal for the re-appointment of the medical officer of health fcr their district for a term of years or permanently, the Board would be prepared to give it consideration. A NURSE'S CHARGE.

With regard to an account of Mr& Eccleshall of 15s. per week for nursing and necessaries ot a patient at the hospital at Moore, and the payment of which had been objected to by Mr. Lister Kaye, Dr. B3wer, of Scretton, wrote informing the Council that the account was in accordance with the terms agreed upon by him with her on the assumption that she was not receiving any remuneration from the union. It had since come to his knowledge that she was receiving .£1 per week for her services at the hospital, and he therefore suggested that the amount be reduced, leaving a nett total of £4 its.—lt was decided that the account be again sent in as origin- ally made to Mr. J.Charlton Parr with an explanation by the Clerk.

THE QUESTION OF AN INFECTIOUS DISEASES FIO;PITAL. • Mr. Roylance wished to know why the smallpox hospi- tal at Moore could not be used for other infectious diseases. There had been a case of scarlet fever at Moore, and owing to there being no hospital the disease had spread, and there were now three or four cases there. It looked strange that a child suffering from fever had been sent by a rich man to the smallpox hospital and yet other persons were not allowed to enter it.—The Chairman said it was a mistake that the child mentioned was ad- mitted to the hospital at all. If it had come before the Authority in the first place it would riot have occurred. —Mr. Roylance moved that the medical :officer and nuisanceinspector visit the infected houses at Moore and report as to their sanitary condition.--It was stated that this would be done in the ordinary course.—Mr. Wood- ward said it might be information ta some members to know that the question of the provision of an inPctious diseases hospital had been before them for eleven or twelve years. A committee had been appointed to deal with the question in accordance with the requirements of the Local Government Board. Vie presumed that the great difficulty now before them was one of a site. The Local Government Board required a site something like a mile from any dwelling, and it was a difficult matter to find such a ene. Three sites had beets submitted for the approval of the Local Government Board. He proposed that the Local Government Board be written to, asking for their decision with regard to the sites submitted to them.—Mr. Heywood seconded the proposition.—Mr. Stokes thought they should have the doctor's opinion as to whether it was not possible for them to use the smallpox hospital as an infectious diseases hospital. He did not make any account of having a building like•that lying idle.—Dr. Adams stated that no self-respecting body would think for a moment of using a wooden building like the stnall-pox hospital for infectious diseases, and further the Local Government Board would not allow them to utilize it in its present condition for such a purpose. It was a great mistake that it had been used in the case cited. He was away at the time or it would not have happened. Had not the child in question been vaccinated it might have had smallpox.—Mr. Stokes : Dan% you think if tne hospital was disinfected and well painted that it would be suitable ?—Dr. Adams said if they used a wooden building for infectious diseases they would have public opinion against them on the ground that it was an in- efficient building.—Mr. Stokes : And yet it was suitable for smallpox ?—Dr. Adams said with regard to small- pox the patients needed as much fresh air as possible, but it was entirely different in cases of other infectious diseases.—The proposition was ultimately r arried. —lt was also decided that the committee appointed to con- sider the question of an infectious diseases hospital be called together at the next meeting of the Council, and that Mr. Roylance be added to the committee.

div.head: TEE SEWERAGE OF WE4TON POINT.
div.p: TEE SEWERAGE OF WE4TON POINT.

Mr. Diggle submitted a plan of the proposed new sewer to be laid at Weston Point.—Mr. Stokes on behalf of the committee appointed to c insider the matter, pro- p... Red that it be now carried out as shown on the plan.—Mr. Aaron seconded the proposition, and said the question had been before them for 20 years.—Mr. Darbyshire thought they should be supplied with further particulars respecting the scheme. He would like to know what the cost would be.—Mr. Diggle estimated that the cost would be about £loo.—Mr. Stokes stated that he wished to add to his proposition that Captain Clarke be written to with reference to a wall that would have to be disturbed in the carrying out of the scheme. Mr. Darlington said the scheme would be a local charge and he thought the Parish Council in the township should be consulted in the matter. The proposition, after further discussion, was carried.

div.head: NEW BUILDINGS AT FRODSHAII.
div.p: NEW BUILDINGS AT FRODSHAII.
Mr. Diggle presented plans for a jun factory proposed to be erected at Frodsham by Mr. Kidd, and also plan of a shop in Loudon-road, Fradsham. The plans were approved of.

div.head: ROAD IMPROVEMENT AT FITS CROSAES.
div.p: A ROAD IMPROVEMENT AT FITS CROSAES.

The report of the Committee appointed to consider the suggested improvement to a road near Mr. Parkinson 8 house, Five Crosses, was presented. Mr. Parkinson offered to give the land requir2d and £5 towards the expense of the erection of a suitabl,t wall, the remainder to be paid by the authority.—Mr. Heywood in moving that the offer be accepted said it would only cost the au- thority .£lo.—Mr. Woodward seconded.—Dr. Darlington moved a negative proposition that the offer be not ac- cepted. Mr. Bradford seconded the amendment, and Mr. Darbyshiro supported it.—Mr. Brandreth spoke in support of the proposition, which was carried on being put to the vote. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Adams reported that in accordance with instruc- tions at the last meeting, he inspected a cottage at Whitley Inferior. The overcrowding, as reported, did exist, out with regard to the dilapidated condition of the house he would suggest that he again see it when the wet weather had set in.He could scarcely conscientiously condemn it at present. Three cases of scarlet fever at Moore had been reported to him and he was now going to investigate them.—The report was adopted.

A KINGSLEY-ROAD. Mr. Woodward submitted the reports of the Commit- tee app.-Anted to consider the question of the widening of Chapel-lane, Kingsley. The Committee admitted the necessity of the improvement and recommended that the tender of Mr. Littler for widening the road be ac- cepted.—Mr. Brandreth seconded the adoption of the committee's report.—Mr. Darlington opp9sed it, but it was carried.

div.head: APPLETON WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: APPLETON WATER SUPPLY.

Writing with reference to this subject, Mr. Thomas Hall. of Birchdale, said he was informed that the Apple- ton Parish Council decided to take no action in carrying out a scheme for supplying Appleton with water since some member had been informed that the Warrington Corporation intended in the near future to give a better supply. Now for five years their complaints had simply been laughed at, first by the Water Company, and latterly by the members of the Water Committee of the Warrineton Corporation. The supply diminished year by year and it had now become so intermittent and de- ficient that it was a mockery to call it a water supple. The responsibility devolved upon the Runcorn Council, and he thought the best pressure they could use was to formulate a scheme for the supply even if they never intended to carry it out since the Warrington Corpora- tion did not want to lose the revenue from Appleton.— Mr. Davenport moved, and Mr. Bradford seconded, that the report be refered to the Appleton Parochial Coin- mittee.—This was agreed to.

RIVER TOLLUTION. The Town Clerk of Warrington (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), writing in reference to the complaints of the Runcorn Council regarding the Stockton Heath outfall, said he was informed by his Parliamentary agent that it was not the intention of Parliament to take opposed business this session, and that his (Mr. Whittle's) bill was opposed by the London and North-Western Ry. Co.,it would have to be held over until the February session and would consequestly lose twelve months. The question was,what was to be done in the meantime for the condition of the river was simply unbearable. He understood that the sluice which was censtrucred by the Ship Canal Corn• pany under the new road at Wilderspool was closed by order of the Acting Conservator of the Mersey, and he was now in communication with the Conservator with the object of coming to some arrangement with regard to the reopening of this sluie. He would keep them in- formed as to the tw,gress made with regard to the mctter. ThP fl neon Coneeil .7,04 ovidPntly rniH- •.l.l, '1 WO teA p lullou o i.e Uhl bell,' of the river at Warrington. The Corporation had no sewer discharging into it. Sonia of the houses on Wilderspool Causeway drained direct into the river but these were single drains and therefore not vested in the Corporation. Would the Runcorn Authority be prepared to join with him in undertaking to construct the sewer arranged to be trade for biking the sewage from Stockton Hesth into the system of sewers within the bornugh on the under• standing that when h? provisional order for the exten- simr of the borough was confirmed by Parliament they should repay the money expended by the Runcorn Authority P T h at would greatly mitigate the nuisance hot it could not be completely c 'red until the authcri- les higher up the river erased to p ',flute it.—Mr. Hey- wood proposed that the letter be reterred to the Appleton Parochial Committee.—Mr. H.rhyshire suggested that the Appleton Committee should act jointly with a com-

mittee of that Council.—Mr. Heywood said he would be pleased to fall in with that suggestion.—Mr. Davenport said the Appleton Parochial Committee would not know what to do in the matter. They would simply forward it to the Council again.—Mr. Derbyshire said it was be- coming a serious question. Houses were becoming empty at Wilderspool and Stockten Heath in consequ- ence of the stench.—Mr. Knowles referred to the import- ance of the sluice being opened again.—Mr. Davenport stated that it was closed because a few manufacturers who used the water for their boilers found it unsuitable for that purpose when the sluice was kept open. The Town Clerk of Warrington in his letter thought he would be able to get it opened again. They at Appleton had been fighting for that for a long time. He proposed that the matter be allowed to hemn abeyance for a short time. and that a letter be forwarded to the Town Clerk of War- rington pressing upon him Me advisability of getting the sluice opened again.—Mr. Darbyshire thought they should take immediate action in the matter.—lnspectot Farrington said the Town Clerk of Warrington stated that there was very little sewage being put into the river by the Corporation at the place mentioned, but he could say there were five or six sewers of the Corporation entering into it.—Mr. Davenport's resolution was ulti- mately carried. COMPLAINT FROM FRODSRAM.

_ ' Mr. Charles Linaker in a communication said he was sorry to have again to complain of the horrible stench arising from the trucks of bones lying in the siding at Frodsham station. It was too bad that the nuisance should remain unabated. He hoped the matter would receive the attention of the Council and that there would be no further need to complain.—lnspector Far- rington stated that he received a copy of the complaint t.nd he went to the station at Frodsham Immediately. He there found two wag,,ons, onf containing a few bones and another filled with small tins of lobster in a state of decomposition. The smell was very bad indeed. Mr. Woodward proposed that the complaint be for- warded to the railway company.--:-This was seconded by Mr. Darbvshire, and carried.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 24, 1895
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 24, 1895
PROPOSED POUT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

In submitting report of Dr. R. Bruce Low, Local Government Board Inspector, on certain circumstances connected with the Manchester Ship Canal, the Local Government Board stated that on consideration of the report, the Board were of opinion that arrangements should now he made for the investigation of the pro- posal that a joint board be constituted to act as Port Sanitary Authority for the Custom's Port of Manches- ter. It appeared to them that it would be necessary for any such Port Sanitary Authority to came to some arrangement with the Port Sanitary Authority of Liver- pool,with a view to the control of infected ships arriving in the Mersey and intending to pass into the Manchester Ship Canal, and also of ships on board of which cholera might arise after they had passed into the canal. Under these circamstances the Board proposed that in the first instance an informal conference of representatives of all the authorities concerned should be called together to meet one of the Board's medical inspectors in order to discuss the question generally in its medical bearings, and they would be glad to learn, as soon as practicable, that, a date convenient to the various riparian authori- ties and to the Port Sanitary Authority of Liverpool had been decided upon.—The Clerk stated that a com- mittee had been appointed to deal with the question,and he thought it would be better to refer the letter to it. The committee consisted of Messrs. Heywood,Prandreth Williams, and Chadwick.—lt was decided on the motion of Mr. Woodward, seconded by Mr. Knowles, that this committee act for the Council in this matter.

MAIN ROADS FOR THE COUNTY COUNCIL. Mr. Woodward brought forward the resolution of which he had given notice that the County Council of Cheshire be requested to take over the following high- ways : The road leading from Halton to the Council's boundary at Bartington, and the one from Acton Bridge to their boundary at Stretton.—Mr. Heywood seconded the resolution.—Mr. Darbyshire contended that it was a wrong principle to be giving up the management of their roads to a body which was so lavish in its expenditure. On the proposition being put to the vote, six voted for it, and four against.—Mr. Baxter, C.C., said he thought the City Council would take over the roads as they were, withont charging the Council anything for putting them in order.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr. Brandreth submitted the report of the Finance Cammittee, and stated that the balance in hand was £2,097 7s. 21. The expenses to be paid amounted to £213 134. 41., of which sum £l7B 9s. 9d. was the half- yearly payment of the Frodsha.m water scheme —Mr. Heywood seconded the adoption of the report, which was carried. NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

Mr. Farrington rAported on the water supply of Grap- penhall. Be asked for permission to take samples of well-water at a number of houses there, for the purpose of analysis.—This was granted.—On his recommenda- tion, a certificate of occupation was issued for a new house at Grlppenhall for Mr. James Kenworthy. This concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE St )CIETY, LIMITED.
div.p: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE St )CIETY, LIMITED.
THE REVISION OF RULES.-AN OTHER P ROMA CTED MEETING.

As was expected, the members of the Runcorn Co-operative Society, Limited, gathered in full force at the Public Flail, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening, when a special meeting for the revision of rules was held. A good number of Widnes members were present, and it will be remembered that at a meeting held in Widnes last week the question of taking steps to sever their con- nection with the society was seriously considered. Their contention is that they are not dealt with justly by the Runcorn members who" boss the show," and scout all their proposals. At the meeting of the committee last week it was decided that the press should not be admitted to the meeting for the revision of rules, and consequently, and perhaps wisely, only members of the society were present. From particulars which have since been gathered, it appears that Mr. Sayles was unanim- ously voted to the chair on the proposition of Mr. Dyer, seconded by Mr. Aston. The Chairman then called upon the Secretary (Mr. Upton) to read the notice convening the meeting. A dis- cussion ensued as to which rules should be read,whether thwe at present in force,nr those which had been revised by the two committees. It was decided on the motion of Mr. Poulson, seconded by Mr. Clarke, after a heated debate, that the rules at present in force should be read, and members should move any amendments to them.

Rule 1, giving the name, place of office, and object of the society was then read. In moving an amendment that the society be called the "Runcorn and Widnes Co- operative Industrial and Provident Society Limited" instead of the "Runcorn Co-operative Industrial and Provident Society Limited "ASit at present stood, Mr. Poulson of Widnes, said he did so with the sole object of promoting the best interests of the society. He argued that Widnes was doing a considerable portion of the business, and he thought it should be recognised in the name of the society. It was only an act of justice.— Mr. Hughes seconded the amendment.—ln supporting it, Mr. Cozier said there was a feeling abroad in Widnes that the Runcorn society was a foreign one. They could disperse that feeling by adding the word "Widnes" in the society's name. Instead of weakening the society, as was contended, it would be strengthening it.— Mr. B. Kniveton said undoubtedly a crisis had arrived in the history of the socie y and the steps taken now would be either for the making or marring of the society. It was quite evident that there was a strong feeling amongst the Widnes members that they should be recognised in the name given to the society. What was in a name ? Would it do the society any harm to let the word " Widnes " be included in the name? He was of opinion that it would allay the strong feeling which existed and tend to restore harmony between the Runcorn and Widnes members. It was not an unusual thing when a business increased to take in another partner,and that was what the Widnes people were ask- ing for. They were doing a large portion of the business and it should be recognised. Thu speakers against the amendment included Mr. Watson and Mr. Worthington. The contention was used that Runcorn had commenced the society and that there was no necessity to change the name. The Widnes members received the same dividend as the Runcorn members. It was moved by Mr. D. Worthington, seconded by Mr. James Johnson that the name remain as at present. A vote was then taken Messrs. J. Stubbs, J. Johnson, Kniveton and Israe Hayes being appointed tellers. For the amendmentl there voted 91, against 138. The amendment was there- fore lost by a majority 0147. Rule 2 was then taken into consideration. A sug- gestion of Mi. Cezier's was accepted and adopted on the motion of Mr. Goodier, seconded by Mr. Eden, that a clause instead of reading " No member shalt be entitled to more than 2 per cent, on his shares," should read "on the whole of his shares."—&n amendment was moved to the clausa stating that no member should hold more than " two " hundred shares. In moving that it should read " one " hundred shares,Mr. Poulson said he did so in the interests csf the poorer members of the society.—Mr. Ford seconded the amendment.—Mr. D. Worthington strongly advocated the retention of two hundred shares,and contended that it had conduced to al great extent to the success of the society.—The amend- Tn.nt waq In.t he 98 votes to 55.—Mr. Kniveton pro- posed the addition of the words "After setting aside 5 per cent, to the reserve fund until the reserve fund amount to £5,000." After the following clause "Each member shall half-yearly, if circumAances will allow thereof, receive out of the surplus receipts of the society (after providing for the expenses) interest, after such rate, not exceeding five per cent, per annum." In doing so he contended that there was no society with the capital and turnover such as they had, with such a small reserve fund. He referred to the bad precedent Set at the annual meeting in touching the reserve fund. —A long and animated discus,ion ensued but ultimately the proposition fell to the ground. It was now nearly ten o'clock, and Mr. Kniveton moved that the meeting he adjourned until the following Tuesday nieht,—Mr. Johnson seconded.—On the proposition being put to the meeting it was carried. . . . .
The Meeting which had lasted three hours was then adjourned.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY OUR RUNCORN CORRRSPONDBNT.

At a special meeting of the Runcorn Co-operative Society on Tuesday evening the vexed question of the rules was discussed almost ad nauseam. None but members were admitted, but from what can be ascertained, the meeting was almost as lively as its predecessor,held a few weeks ago. There was quite a flood of talk but very little business got through. Only two of the rules were considered and revised, and this is all that can be shown for three hours' work. An adjournment was' made until next Tues- day, when the revision of rules will be again pro- ceeded with. If last Tuesday's progress is not ac- lelerated, the work of revision is not only going to be a laborious one, but a costly affair to the Society.

The crux of the whole difficulty which has arisen seems to be the discontentment which prevails amongst the members of the society on the Lanca- shire side of the river. They seem to be dissatisfied with the way they are treated by the Runcorn members who out-vote them. Their proposals,they contend, are defeated by the Runcornians, and in consequence of being unable to get a fair share of representation upon the committee, their voice in the society's management is seldom heard. These objections do not seem too formidable to be sur- mounted, and it will be a great pity if they lead to a complete severance of the Lancashire members from the society. Tnere must be give and take on both sides if they are to act in co-operation. What, for instance, does it matter if the society is called the " Runcorn Co-operative Society" instead of, as the Widnesians suggest, the" Runcorn and Widnes Co-Jperativ*Society," or even vice versa ! And yet over this very trivial matter there was a long wrangle at the meeting on Tuesday. Surely the matters in dispute could be settled in an amicable manner by a conference of delegates from both sides of the river.

There were several important matters discussed at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural Council on Tuesday. The question of the provision of an in- fectious diseases hospital for the district was raised and a general opinion seemed to prevail amongst the members that this long felt want should be sup- plied. The cost of such an institution was not lest sight of, and in this respect, a number of members were very desirous of being economical. The Council, of course, is in possession of a wooden building which has been used for a small-pox hospital by them, and now that fortunately we are free from that disease in the district, some of the members were inclined to utilise it for other infec- tious diseases. The impropriety of doing any such thing was pointed out by the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Adams). It would be scarcely possible to make a wooden building free from draughts, and further there was just a likelihood that a patient when installed in this small-pox hospital might be- come a victim to small-pox. It was eventually decided by the Council that a committee should fully consider the matter.

Another matter of importance, and one aff,cting Runcorn, was the suggestion of the Local Govern- ment Board for the formation of a Port Sanitary Authority,to consist of representatives of the ripar- ian authorities in the port of Manchester. With the opening of the Manchester Ship Canal, Runcorn and other places comprising the port of Manchester have been placed in direct communication with foreign ports and vessels arriving therefrom cannot altogether be expected to have perfect immunity from disease. Hence the necessity of a responsible authority for dealing with and checking the pro- gress of any such diseases. The matter has already been discussed at a meeting of representatives of the authorities concerned, and ere long it is ex- pected that some definite arrangements will be made.

A very satisfactory rep r 1 of the year's work at the Runcorn Free Library was presented at a meeting of the Library Committee on Wednesday, and there was ample evidence to show, that the efforts'put forth for tt e diffusion of knowledge in Runcorn are appreciated and taken advantage of by the inhabitants. Apart from the issue of books, which, although large, leaves room for further im- provement, a gratifying feature is the formation of the musical library,for which over 200 v•Aurnes have been purchased, comprising the principal oratorios and operas. That a good number of the inhabitants are musically inclined is attested by the successful musical societies in our midst, and this latest, ad- junct to the library will no doubt be made much use of. No mention was made in the report of the decision to reduce the fee for the loan of books to residents in outlying districts, bat probably there will be more to say about this and its eff let, in the next report.

div.head: ttUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: ttUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.
ANNUAL REPORT.

A meeting of tfia.iii;;;CC;rt-a----PrW: Library Committee was held in the Board room at the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, and there were also present, Messrs. William Handley,W. Hankinson, S. Pope, W. J. Cunningham and Mr. J. D. Jones (librarian). The thirteenth annual report of the committee for the year ending June 30th, 1895, was submitted, from which it appeared that the number of borrowers of hocks during the year was 700, being a decrease of 16 as compared with last year. The library had .been opened for the issue at books 247 days and 22,582 books had been given out during the year, being an increase of 1.378 on last year's issues. Tin:re had been added to the library dur- ing the year 546 volumes, 428 of which had been pur• chased and 118 presented. The total number of volumes in the library was now 7.859. The interest taken in music in the town had led the committee to attempt the formation of a musical library and 207 volumes of music had been purchased. They comprised some of the most important oratorios and operas, and altogether furnished a respectable beginning of what it was to be hoped might become a useful department of the library. A course of six short lectures was delivered in the reading room during the winter months under the title of "Half hours in the Library about books and authors," and considering the poor accommodation furnished in the readingroom, they were a great success. The lec- turers and subjects were as follaiws :—Rev.Canon Wood, M.A., " A few hints be readers" ; Rev. J. S. Simpson, " A Scottish Dickens" ; qr. J J. Ole (librariao.Bootle), "William Cowper " ; Mr. James Wilding. Ruskin's "Seven Lamps of Architecture " ; Mr. William Handley, "James Brindley " ; Rev. W. H. Stables, "A talk with Boys." The reading rcoms were (-Islip frequented by a large number of readers, and sometimes in the evening they were inconveniently crowded. The committee again expressed their thanks to the various donors for their valuable gifts of money, books, periodicals, and news- papers. Tnereport,which was considered highly satis- factory, was adopted and ordered to be printed, en the the motion of Mr. William Handley, seconded by Mr. Pope.

div.head: ISSUES DURING JULY.
div.p: THE ISSUES DURING JULY.

The lending library was opened sixteen times during July. The total issue of books was 1,071 or a decrease of 441 as compared with the corresponding month last year. The books were distributed as follows : Theoloey 13, philosophy 5, science 33, history &c., 73, poetry 9, fiction 818, miscellaneous 116, music 4.—The report was adopted.

div.head: LIBRARY ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE LIBRARY ASSOCIATION.

A communication was read from this association,stat- inv,, that the 18th annual meeting of the Library Associa- tion of the United Kingdom would be held at Cardiff from September 10th to 13th.—It was decided that the Librarian should attend on behalf ef the Committee And that his expenses to the extent of £5 be paid, as was the case last year.—Mr. William Handley was also asked to attend at his own expense. This was all the business of public interest. HALTON.

WESLEYAN SIINDAY Scnoot.—The juvenile branch of the Missionary Society held a meeting in the above school on Sunda), afternoon. The chair was occupied by Mr. C.?. Bradbury. The secretary (Mr. Moors) read a very encouraging report of the work done during the year, and Messrs. W. Rowe, C. Smith, J.L. Saunders, J. Clarke, and A. Baguley delivered appropriate addresses. The following mutiical programme was gone through ; Solo "All my doubts I give to Jesus," Miss C. Looker : duet, " The Gfr tner," Miss A. Lloker and Miss A. Saunders : quartette, " 'the Village Church," Messrs. W. Rowe and C. P. Bradbury, Miss A. Looker and Miss M. Newport ; solo, "To Thy cross I cling," Miss Boys, who also acted as accompanist. A good collection was taken. WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—The anntral trip to Over- ton Hills took place on Saturday afternoon. The party consisting of about 110 ciildren and 50 adults, was con- veyed in Messrs. Booth and Son's wagonettes. Tea was partaken of at Mersey View. The weather was beauti- fully fine, and a very enjoyable time was spent. This society, thanks to the enthusiasm of its workers, is in a very flourishing condition, there being a membership of 98.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
DEATH OF MR. WILLIMI HOWARD.

Many will regret to bear of the death of Mr. William Howard, late of Victoria-road, Runcorn, who died at Chester Asylum, on Wednesday. The deceased gentle- man was well known in the town, and for many years was a prominent member of the Runcorn Parish Church choir. _ _ _

BRUNSWICK BOYS' Scßoot, RUNCORN. The report of the recent drawing examination is just to hand and shows that this school, which is under the headmaStership of Mr. B. Crosby, has for the sixth time, received the excellent award for drawing. _ A SUCCESSFUL STUDENT. .

In the pass list containing the of the junior candidates who satisfied the examiners at the Oxford local examinations held in July, appears the name of G. P. Williams of Runcorn. There were 1,200 candidates.
BOWLING MAIN AT RUNCORN.

A bowling contest among the members of the Bridge Hotel Club was held on Saturday. The green was in first-class condition and the result of the contest was as follows :-Ist prize H. Wright, 2nd T. Woods, 3rd H. Treadwell, 4th Kay, sth Riley and 6th Milliner. SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT.

The scholars connected with the Nelson-st. Wesleyan Sunday school, to the number of about one bundred,had their annual treat on Thursday afteraoon. They pro- ceeded by train to Sutton Weavor and thence to a fiPld, where various games were engaged in. Tea was pro- vided, and a happy time was spent. ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN CHEMICAL WORKER.

On Thursday afternoon, an accident befell Joseph Davies, of 12 Eaton-street, Runcorn, whilst following his employment in one of the chemical yards at Widnes. It appears that he slipped into a vat of liquid, and both of his legs were burnt as far as the knees. They were wrapped up in sacking, and he was carried home across the bridge.
SCALDING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

About noon on Thursday, a child named Calvert Grisdale, aged eleven months, son of Mr. William Grisdale, of 12, York-street, Runcorn, died from the effects of scalding. The child received its injuries on Tuesday evening when during the engagement of the mother in culinary work,the child upset a pan of boiling water. the contents scalded its back severely. Medi- cal aid was immediately procured but the child expired. as stated on Thursday. An inquest will probably be held to-day (Friday).

div.head: ViORANCY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ViORANCY AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. F. J. Norman, John Lawton, of Percival-lane, Runcorn, was charged with sleeping out in Duke's stables at about 130 that morninz.—P.C. Gregory proved the charge. The prisoner had been previously dealt with for a similar offence, and in committing him to prison for seven days, the magistrate warned him that if he appeared again before the Bench, he would be more severely dealt with.

div.head: LANDING OF EHEEP AT RUNCORN-.
div.p: LANDING OF EHEEP AT RUNCORN-.

A steamer arrived in the canal at Runcorn on Sunday night about nine o'clock, having on board a large num- ber of sheep and other cattle for disembarkation at Run- sorn, Manchester, and intermediate places. She was moored at the Old Quay, Runcorn, and the consignment for Runcorn consisted of 250 sheep for a farmer at Kings- ley. Doubts were entertained as to the possibility of landing the animals at Runcorn, but Captain Heasley, superintendent of the Runcorn section, made every necessary arrangement for the disembarkation of the flock, and it is to his credit that this was accomplished without the slightest mishap. _

PARISH CHURCH CHOIR AND BIBLE CLASS PICNICS. Upwards of 40 members of the choir connected with the Runcorn Parish Church had a picnic to Blackpool on Saturday morning. An enjoyable time was spent in Blackpool in the morning,and a drive to the Strawberry Gardens was participated in, in the afternoon. Mr. J. Littler, (the choirmaster) made excellent arrangements. —Those connected with the Vicar's Bible Class proceeded to Eaton Hall on Saturday afterneon. In the absence of the Vicar, the party was accompanied by the Rev. H. B. Firth, and also by Mr. John Littler. They took train to Chester, and then went up the Dee to Eaton Hall. They rambled through the park and also visited the hall. Tea was partaken of at Earlestown Perry.

div.head: OPENING OF THE TECHNIC-AL INSTITUTE.
div.p: THE OPENING OF THE TECHNIC-AL INSTITUTE.

Mr.Marshall,thP enerffetic secretary of the Tecbnical In- stitute is now tn. king every arrangement for the success- ful opening of the Institute which is to take plekce on Seurday afternoon, August 31st. Sir John T. Brunner,Bart., perform the opening ceremony. There will be a grand procession from Devonshire- square at four o'clock, and the streets to be paraded will be found in an advertisement, and the townspeople are respectfully asked to decorate the houses and streets en route. On arrival at the Institute the ceremony of opening will be proceeded with. At seven o'clock a free concert is to be held. Persons coming from a distance will be provided with a lunch, and those who intend coining would do well to put themselves in communica- tion with Mr. Marshall, the secretary, at an early date.

div.head: RUNCORN' _POLICE COV-R.T.
div.p: RUNCORN' _POLICE COV-R.T.

At this Court on Tuesday mcrning, before Mr. F. J. Norman, a middle-aged man named Robert McCulloch, who stated that he belonged to Belfast, was charged with begging in Church-street the previous night.—P.C. Wright proved the charge, and stated that when he searched the prisoner he found in his possession seven- pence in money and a quantity of food.—The magis- traUs stated that he had received a notice from the Runc)rn Guardians, urging him to deal severely with such men as the prisoner. There was no necessity to beg when he had money and food in his possession. Ele would be committed to prison for seven days hard labour—At the same court on Wednesday morning, Levi Barnett of Farnwortb, was fined ss. including costs for being drunk at Runcorn, the previous night.

div.head: PICNIC OF BRIDGE WATER CANALS EMPLO-YES.
div.p: PICNIC OF BRIDGE WATER CANALS EMPLO-YES.

A picnic, the-first of its kind, in connection with the blacksmiths, boilersmitlm, copper and tinsmiths employed at the Victoria Yard, Runcorn, of the Bridge- water Canals undertaking, was held on S4turday. The party, numbering 44, was conveyed to Chester in brakes supplied by Messrs. T. Booth and Sons, of Runcorn. On arrival at Chester, about one o'clock, dinner was pro- vided, to which full justice was done. Places of interest in the ancient city were next visited, Messrs. W. Moston (foreman), S. Blundell, T. Millington and J. J. Gittens conducting the party. The sail to Eccleston Ferry was fully appreciated, and a visit was afterwards paid to Eaton Hall. On returning to Chester they again resorted to the Woolpack Hotel, arid enjoyed the able catering of the host, Mr. S. Davies, formerly of Runcorn. A stroll leisurely through the town was taken prior to the depar- ture for home, which was reached about eleven o'clock. The day's outing was thoroughly enjoyed.

div.head: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY'S EXCIIRSTON.
div.p: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY'S EXCIIRSTON.

The popular annual excursion in connection with the Runcorn Co-operative Society, Limited, was held on Monday. Blackpool was the place decided upon to be visited,and the number of excursionists totalled 500 from the Runcorn side,and about 250 from the Widnes &s- -trict. The train departed from Runcorn promptly at 6.40 a.m. and arrived at the place ot destination about 9.45. They then dispersed themselves in various direc- tions, many proceeding to the shore at once. The Tower proved a great attraction, and many patronised the Winter Gardens and the Baths, the excursionists being admitted to the latter place at reduced rates. The return journey was commenced about seven o'clock,and home was reached at 9.45, which was considered very good time. The day was beautifully fine, and it is a matter of course to say that the trippers greatly enjoyed themselves. The Runcorn football players also accom- panied the excursion. The arrangements were made by the committee of the society consisting of Messrs. Rhodes, Rogerson, Worthingtor„ Sayles, Aston, Dyer, Riley, and Dudley. _

div.head: RUNCORN POOR CHILDREN'S TREAT.
div.p: RUNCORN POOR CHILDREN'S TREAT.

The poor children of Runcorn, were on Wednesday afternoon provided with their annual treat, and the ' event was favoured with propitious weather. A special train conveyed the youngsters,who.seemed in high glee, to Frodsham. They then marched off to Overton Hill, where they spent a merry time until tea was served at Mersey View. Over 600 children sat down, and their , wants were attended to by a host of workers. Amongst those present were the Revs. Dr. Gastaldi, Father Byrne ' (Widnes), H. B. Firth, F. C. Movie, Messy:. W. Shaw (missionary), S. Coventry, J. W. Wood land,E. Marshall, M. Sweetman, J. C. Williams, P. Leathwood. Leach, T. Reynolds, T. Wood, T. Bowyer, G. Howard, J. D. Jones T. Cooke, and W. Millington (secretaries),Miss C. Littler, Mrs. T. Bowyer, Mrs. T. Wood, Mrs. T. Reynolds, Mrs. W. Shaw, Misses Comerford, Miss Bowyer, Miss Forster, Mrs. G. Howard, Mrs. H. Shaw,and Mrs. F. C. Williams. The St. Edward's League of the Cross band,which kindly accompanied the children, played several selections dur- ing the afternoon. Mr. Quinn was the conductor. A number of races were held, the prizes consisting of a number of toys, being provided by Mr. T. Wood. A quantity of nuts and sweets, sent by Mr. T. Lead were scattered amongst the children. At seven o'clock they started for the railway station, and entrained at 7.30. The outing was greatly enjoyed. RUNCORN SCHOOL HOARD SCIENCR AND ART CLASSES. div.head: INTERESTING PRESENTATIONS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: INTERESTING PRESENTATIONS AT RUNCORN.

Musa Florence Whitney, daughter of Mr. Whitney, of Runcorn, was the recipient of several presents on Sun- day from those connected with the United Methodist Free Church and school on her departure from Runcorn for Stanford, Maine, U.S.A. The present from members of the congregation consisted of a Bible and hymn book, and that from the Young People's Christian Endeavour, a valuable book. The Sunday school class with which Miss Whitney was connectectpresented her with a purse of money. The presentations were made with the best wishes of her future welfare and success. Miss Whitney suitably acknowledged the gifts. SERIOUS ACCIDENTS TO RUNCORN YOUTHS.

About a score oi children were, on Friday evening, playing on a railing erected oa an embankment near to the Manchester Ship Canal, and opposite South Bank Terrace, Runcorn. Suddenly the fence gave way and they were prec•pitated down the embankment. Five youths were seriously injured about the head, arrns,and back. Their injuries were attended to by Dr. Gilchrist locum tenens for Dr. McLennan, and Dr. Robinson. One of them named Alrinson was badly hurt on the head and was unconscious for some time. They are all now, however, recovering from their injuries.

div.head: MERSEY MISSION TO. SEAMEN.
div.p: MERSEY MISSION TO. SEAMEN.

The Sunday school anniversary services in connec- tion with the Runcorn branch of this mission were held on Sunday. In the morning Mr. William Shaw preached to a fair congregation. A service of song entitled "Little Pilgrim" was exceedingly well rendered in the afternoon. The children, who had bean trained by Mr. Price and Miss Bowyer, recited and sang various pas- sages, whilst the choir sang the choruses. Mrs.R. Shaw also contributed a solo. The music was made addition- ally attractive by an augmented band, the performers consisting of a number of members of the Runcorn Volunteer Rand. The Rev. Edgar Lambert, M.A., the newly appointed chaplain of the mission conducted the service, and in the course of a short address,said he was glad to see the number of workers in the school which was being so successfully carried on. The rev.gentleman also preached to a large congregation in the evening. The collections, which were in aid of the school funds, realised a satisfactory amount. ACCIDENT AT THE DOCKS.

A workman at the Runcorn Docks, named Walker, 2, Ashridge-st.,met with an accident whilst at work on Thursday afternoon. It appears that he was working in a truck,when he was struck by the apparatus used in loading it. He crag knocked out of the wagon and fell to the ground. He was picked up and conveyed home. Dr. McKenzie was immediately sent for,and on examin- ing the man he fonnd him to be suffering from a scalp wound, and fracture of the right collar-bone. The wound was stitched up, and the man lies in a serious condition.

div.head: RUNCORN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB,
div.p: RUNCORN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB,

This club has now almost completed its list of fixtures for the forthcoming season. The club increased its popularity in Runcorn last season, and there is every probability that this year it will be still more successful. Inclusion has been eff -,cted in the Warrington and Dis- trict Association LeaguP, and the first match is to be played on the second Saturday in September when War- rington will be the visitors.

div.head: FREEMASONRY.
div.p: FREEMASONRY.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A rneetine of this Board was held in the Board Room, at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afterno.m. Mr. J. W. Knowles occupied the chair, and there were also pre- sent in addition to the members of the Runcorn Rural Council, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. S. Yarwood, Mr. Ashton (clerk). Mr. G. A,hron (deputy Clerk), and Mr. Cunnah (Workhouse 'easter).

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

_ Mr. Heywood, in submitting the report of the Finance Committee, said they had signed cheques to the amount of £3,320, of which £3,155 was for the County Council call, and the remainder was chiefly for out relief. The balance in hand was only £1,073, but they were signing the cheques and leaving them in the Clerk's hands against the time the townships paid their calls.—Mr. Brandreth wished to know what was the total call of the County Council for the half year.—Mr. Heywood re- plied that it was £4,175, the heaviest call which they had ever received from the County Council. The calls were due on the 16th August, but the only township which had paid was Weston, which was very creditable to that township.—MtWondward seconded the adoption of the report which was carried.

div.head: NEW STATION.
div.p: A NEW STATION.

Mr. De Prez introduced the question of the advisa- ‘)ility of establishing a station for the purposes of relief and vtccioation for the three townships added to the Union. Re suggested that a room near Grappenhall Church be rented.—This was agreed to.

div.head: THR HALTON ALLEGED THEFT CASE.
div.p: THR HALTON ALLEGED THEFT CASE.

Mr. Cooke, in submitting his out-relief report,referred to the case of Ann Collier, of Halton, who had for years been receiving weekly out-relief. In a police case which had occurred,the officer who searched the house in which Miss Collier lived, stated that he found a bag containing gold, and that she claimed it as hers. When he (Mr. Cooke) heard of it,he made it his business to visit Ann Collier. She show(' him the bag mentioned and all that it contained was 503., and she denied that there was any more in it when the officer came to the house. She also made the same statement to Mr. Allen, solicitor. As she could not be considered destitute, he (Mr. Cooke) had discontinued the out-relief for the present. He did not think it was possible for them to get any of the money paid to her, returned.—lt was decided to uphold the action of Mr. Cooke.

TREAT TO THE INMATES. A vote of thanks was accorded the Nrodsham band for entertaining the inmates of the workhouse with music, and also to the Frodsbam Guardians for feasting them on an occasion a few days ago. This concluded the business.

div.head: MUSIC IN THR PARK..
div.p: MUSIC IN THR PARK..
The Warrington PoQtal Band will occupy the stand in the Park on Monday, at 7 p.m., when a selection ot dance music will be given.
Winiacnoss ROPERY l'icruC.

The sth annual picnic of the Whitecross Repery took place on Sunday. The party started at 8 a.m. from Mr. Connors Sankey-street, in a iiloon brake. The route taken was through Northwieh to Kiwis- ford where a good dinner was provided by Mr. Drinkwater of the Freemasons' Arms, which was very much enjoyed. After dinner a ramble through the park of Lord Egerton at Tatton Hall and round the Heath brought the day's proceedings to a close. The party returned home about nine o'clock after a most enjoyable day.

Terrific thunderstorm were experienced in 'various parts ot the country on Thursday morning, Several lives were lost, and /14113e9 and other buildings, as well as corn stacks, set on fire by lightening and destroyed. The first-class British battleship Prince George, 14,500 tons, or 500 tons heavier and nearly 40 feet longer than the Royal Sovereign, was launched from Portsmouth Dockyard on Thursday.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
HALF-YEARLY MEETING OF SHAREHOLDERS:
THE DIRECTORS' REPORT.
• The Dire:ttors' report which was submitted to the half yearly meeting of shareholders on Tuesday has beea is— sued. It is as follows :

The expenditure on Capital account during the half year, after deducting proceeds of sales of plant and land was £115.175, making a total expenditure out of capital of £14,948,552, and leaving a balance on that account of £458,447.

The receipts on Ship Canal revenue account amounted to £63,036, and the exnPnditure, including £8,910 for maintenance, to £s6,ooB,leaving a balance of £7,028. The profits of the Bridgewater undertaking amounted t" £18,239, giving a total balance of £25,267. The following are the details of the net revenue account :—At the commencement of the half-year the credit balance carried forward amounted to £155,689, to which are added the profits for the .half-year £25,267, and the balance of the general interest account £4,186, making a total of £185,142; after charging interest due on mortgage debentures for the half-rear, viz., £160,840, there remains a credit balance of £24,502 to be carried forward.

In the general bslance sheet there is on the 3ebter side an entry of £112,500 appearing as owing to the Man- chester Corporation,but one-half of the ain0unt,£.93,250. was paid on the 3rd July. The Cm.poration, having regard to the financial position of the company, and the necessity for further expenditure on equipment, acceded to the request of the direc'ors to al:ow the remaining half of the accrued interest to remain in arrears mean while.

SFIIP CANAL TRAFFIC. The receipts from the Ship Canal undertaking amounted to £62,810, an increase eomnared with the corresponding six months of 1894 of £19,498. although the receipts from passengers were less by £3,401. Ex- cluding passengers, who cannot be regarded as a large permanent source of revenue, the increase was E 22,897.
The weight of merchandise paying tolls which passed over the Ship Canal during the two periods was as fol- lows :
Six months ending June 30, 1895. June 30, 1894. Tons. Tons. In sea-going craft 480.784 In barges

Total The increase is, on toe a7erage, steady and coatinu- ous. No effort is being spared.and an established foot- ing has been obtained in many of the trades of the dis- trict, but circumstances beyond the control of the com- pany cause delay in some directions.

div.head: BRIDGEWATER UNDERTAKING.
div.p: BRIDGEWATER UNDERTAKING.

The net revenue from this undertaking was £18,239 as compared with £20.024 for the came period last year. This result is satisfactory in view of the fact that the logs caused by the prolonged frost is estimated at £11,500, mainly diminished revenue, but partly expen- diture to k.,ep the navigation open as long as possible. If that mstortune had not cccurred the result would have been very good for the first six months of the year. The directors are glad to ne able to report that the traffic of the Bridgewater undertaking for the current half-year is being well maintained.
PARLIAMENTARY BUSINESS. As an amicable arrangement was inddr with the Man- _ _ _

cliester Ship Canal Ponricion and Dry Docks Company, Limited, unde* which the pontoon at Ellesmere Port. will be removed from the canal into a recesq now being constructed, the Bill referred to in the report for the previous half-year was withdrawn.

div.head: DIRECTORS.
div.p: DIRECTORS.
Since the last meeting Mr. Henry C. Pingstone has been appointed by the Directors represen, ing the share- holders to the seat on the Board vacant by the lamented death of Sir Joseph C. Lee.
Issued by order ot the Board this 17th day of August, 1895.
JOHN K. BYTHELL, Chairman.
THE FOLLOWING IS THE ENGINEETLS' REPORT AS TO THE
PROGRESS OF THE WORKS.

The deposits of silt which had accumulated in the tidal portion of the Carat during construction have been to a great extent removed, and the rem dnder, together with the more recent deposits brought into the Canal, mainly through the tidal openings, is now in process of removal. The recent heavy rains have c4used a further deposit of sewage sludge, &c., in the upper portion of the Canal, which is also being removed by the dredgers. The three pairs ot large three storeyed sheds at the Docks have been completed and equipped,and are being used for traffic purposes. The railway swing bridge at Trafford-road has been fin,shed and opened for traffic. A large arca of addi- tional paving has been carried out at the docks, and extensive railway sidings have been laid down, besides which a further area of quay sp nee has been levelledand utilised for the timber trade. The works for a new hydraulic installation at Mode Wheel and the perman- ent electric liglating ot the !Manchester docks, have been commenced.

'The timber wharf and jetties at Mode Wheel for the cattle lairages, constructed tor the Manchester Corpora- tion, have been completed and are reads' fr use. The dolphins below and above EisLlatn Locks have been completed. Operations have been commenced hr the removal of the pontoon at Ellesmere Port, and for the construction of additional deep-water jetties and a coal tip at Runcorn.
Various other works necessary for the equipment of the Canal and docks have also been compl, ted, and some others are in progress.

Considerable additions have been made to the protec- tive work of the Canal slopes, and the slopes generally are in much better order. The works generally throughout the Canal have been efficiently maintained and are now in good order. W. HENRY HUNTER, Engineer of the Company. Manchester, 14 h August, 1895. At the half-I e.irly meeting of shareholders held on Tuesday, Mr. J. K Byt hell (chairman of tie. Company) presided. In moving the adoption of the Directors' report and balance-sheet, the Chairman said the past half year had been taken up with .Keafly, continuous work,and with ii consistent endeavour to obtain a steady footing with the various trades o' the district. Many of their most serious difficulties had been r-m,ved. If the example of the Manchester Corporation, not alone in giving financial aid, but in affording facilities for traffic and extending the weight of its in fl leiter. in every direc- tion, were followed by the trading community, the 1, difficulties of the Company would very soon disappear ' andlrapid headway would be made. When, what he might term thf•educational process was further advanced and when the whole of the mercantile community real- ised what the canal, with the general co-operation of traders, could do for the district, they might be sure the Company would make more rapid strides. Adverting to the friendly arrangement which the Company bad made vrth Warrington and Run- corn, the Chairman expressed great. pleasure at being able to say that the Company werrr now practi- call; rid of all those obligations which menaced them aforetime, and might have led to a further serious drain on their resources. He was sorry to sic that the rail- way rates to and from the docks were tv t vet settled, and that the Company would have to tight the matter out before the Railway Commissioners. All they desired was that the port of Manchester should be put in an equally favourable position with other ports, looking at its geographical position • and they musL at all risks contend for, or they would have no chance of develop- ing anything like a large traffic. In conclusion Mr. Bythell made a powerful appeal to traders to take ad- vantage of the facilities afforded by the canal, and thereby benefit not only themselves but toe shareholders of the Company arid the ratepayers of Manchester in general. Hc remarked that it was only through the failure of tra 'era in this respect that a pecuniary burden would before long fall upon the ePlz-ns in order that the Corporation might have funds to meet toe claim for in- terest on the money borrowed and lent to the Canal Company. The resolution adopting the report was un- animously adopted. A few questions haviagbeenput and answered, the meeting terminated.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT.

" - FRIDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Dr. Gornall, Alderman Wright. NinatEcT OF WORE BY AN APPRENTICE.—Fanny Regan, Dial Court, was summoned for leaving her work while being in the employ of Harriet Ann Mills, and thereby causing a loss ot sa.—She was ordered to return to work and pay 61. a week till the sum was paid off. SENT TO THE CLlO.—William Dennett, 21 Lord Nelson- street, was summoned for neglecting to sent his child John to school. Application was nakde for him to be sent to the "din," as he was an incorrigible truant. The father objected but the magistrates over-ruled his objec- tion and the boy was sent to the ship until he attained the age of 16 A SERIOUS CASE.—Mary Gleeson, 19 Dutton-at., was charged with assaulting and beating Catherine Robin- son, 18 Dutton-st., on the 9th inst.—Mr. Browne ap- peared for the complainant, who was suffering from a broken arm which it was alleged the defendant had caused by striking the complainant with a brush-stail. Mr. Browne siid that if defendant would pay £lO com- pensation they would withdraw the charge otherwise he would ask that defendant be committed to the Quarter Sessions on a charge of committing bodily harm. Ulti- mately the case was adjourned for a fortnight. A Nom. Tt7r oF Wee.—Elannah Edison, 20,Ha11-st., was charged with assaulting and beating Susan Emmess, 9, Hall-stteet, on the 10th August. There was a cross- summons against Emmess for assaulting Ellison.—Mr. Browne appeared for the complainant and, after ex- plaining that they were rival coal dealers, said that on the day named a little boy wae going to Mrs. E:nmess's place for coal when defendant rushed out and dragged him away. Both caught hold of him and defendant was the first to let go,and she then struck complainant and knocked her to the floor cutting her arm and causing a hair-pin to be knocke I into her head. A sister of the defendant supported this statement.—Mr. F. R. Roberts,: who represented the defendant, said that it was altogether a most trumpery charge. Both women,l he said, were tugging at the boy and his client let go whereupon complainant fell on her back dragging the troy with her. They totally denied the assault.—The boy in question who was only 7 years of age was called and said that he was going to Mrs. Ellison's for coal when the complainant called to him and both of them got hold of him. Mrs. Ernmess fell, she was not struck. Two other witnesses gave evidence for the defence and stated that they saw the whole proceed- ing and supported Mr. Roberts' contention.—The magis- trates dismissed the case, Mr. Harrison observing that both parties were to blame but he thought the complain- ant hal fallen to the ground through defendant releasing the boy. SHORT OF SHELTER.—John Phillips, no address, was charged with absenting himself from the training of the 4th Manchester Militia this year. A sergeant from Orford barracks deposed that prisoner came to him on Thursday night and gave himself up as an absentee.—ln court prisoner said he did so because he wanted shelter. He was remanded till Monday for enquiries to be made. 1 VIOLENCE —Joseph Ward, 9 Winson-square, was charged with assaulting and beating Sarah Hughes, 11, Williamson-Qqua re, on Saturday. Defendant did not appear.—Mrs. Hughes, an elderly woman, stated Ufa defendant struck her and called her foul names.—A ' warrant was granted for his arrest.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (chairman), Alderman Har- rison, Mr. F. Monks, and Mr. J. W. Hayward. THE HOT WEATHER AND ITS RESULTS.—The close weather which extended over the week end was respon- sible for an unusual number of cases of intemperance. before the magistrates on Monday. The follow- ing are the defendants dealt with for being drunk and disorderly :—John Seddon, Hill-st., Sc. including costs ; William Connor, 30, Dolman's-lane (35th appearance), 6s. and costs ; John Fleming. 8, Dial Court, SA. and costs ; Thomas Farrington, 14, Oliver-at., ss. and costs ; John Lang, tramp and beggar, no address, sent to gaol for one month with h labour ; Patrick Kilroy-, 16, Rose aed Crown•st. (19',;h appearance), ss. and costs ; Thomas Fallon, 13, Garden Row, ss. including costs; James Bate, 8, Morris Square, Silver-st., 2s. 6.1. includ- ing costs ; Thomas Brady, Percival's Fold, ss. including costs ; Kate Hines, 8, Hill-At., Si. and costs ; Kate Smith, 14, Silver-square, dismissed. A NEGLECTFUL Hum:tat-tn.—Charles Littlewood, 69, Chorley-st.,was charged on a warrant with having on the 13th August unlawfully neg- lected his wife and children, thereby caus- ing them to become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. B. Shearer, en- quiry officer, stated that a week ago the prisoner's wife applied with her children, for admission to the workhouse. On enquiry they found that two of the children were working and the rest dependent upon their parents, and also that prisoner had had regular work but had gone on the spree at the election and lost his job. Since then hiA family had been nearly starving. —Ur. Garnett, workhouse official, stated that on Tues- day morning, last week, he visited the prisoner's house and found the family entirely without food and fire. Be bad to give them relief at once.—Sergeant Cheney said he apprehended prisoner on Sunday morning at his home. He was lying on the sofa and apparently drunk. Prisoner's wife told him that she had had 24. given her for food and he had taken it and spent it in driidx. Prisoner, who appeared very repentant, confessed that he had given way to drink and begged the indulgence of the Bench, adding that if he went to gaol he would not recover from it. He had lived 34 years in Warrington and never been in a similar positopn.—Mrs. Littlewood, In answer to a query from the Bench, said prisoner had been neglecting her for the last three years.—He was sent to gaol for one month's hard labour, the magistrates remarking that they thought it the kindest thing for him. .

Company Rifle Brigade stationed at Alder- shot, since July.—Detective Monaghan proved the case and said that prisoner had enlisted in the name of John Davies.—He was remanded to Strangeway's Gaol lo await an escort, and Monaghan was awarded the usuat reward for his capture. THEFT FROM A CRICKET PAVILION.—WiIIiam Brown was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Wed- nesday: he was also charged with stealing from the Y.M.C.A. cricket pavilion at Arpley, a pair of braces and a pair of goloshes, the property of Frederick Page. —The Chief Constable stated that the complainant was the captain of a cricket club having a pavilion in Arpley fields. Defendant was a farm labourer or navvy, and had no address. The pavilion in question was locked up securely on Tuesday and on Wednesday morn- ing at 10.30, Henry Woods, workman, was in the neighbourhood of the pavilion and saw the defend- ant pulling at the shutters. Afterwards he saw de- fendant move a concrete step from the door of the pavilion, under which he crawled. About 10 minutes later defendant emerged with a bulkier appearance than 'before. Woods followed him to Mersey-street, and saw defendant enter Leslie's second hand clothes shop. He then went away and informed Detective-Sergeant Mona- ghan who subsequently apprehended defendant in Buttermarket-st. The articles were found at Leslie's and traced to defendant. Corroborative evidence hav- ing been given the magistrates sent defendant to gaol for one month's hard labour. _ .
_ AN ABSENTEE.—AIfred Cannel! was charged with ab- senting himself from the training of the 3rd Liverpool Militia this year. He pleaded guilty and was handed over to the military authorities.

AN INGENIOUS DEFENCE. —Ellis Scott, a respectable looking woman, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Marsh House-lane early on Thursday morn- ing.—Sergeant Smith and P.C. Evans proved the case, but prisoner for her defence said she heard Smith say to the constable "Well both lock her up and then we'll have a case." (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Hunt observed that it was evidently not the first time the prisoner had been in a police court.—She was fined ss. and costs.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WiIIiam Hopley, a young man residing at 21, Cliff View Cottages, vrodsham, was fined ss. including costs for being drunk and disorderly in Greenway-road, Runcorn, on the 11th August.—P.C. Richardson proved the case. LlCENSlNG.—Permission was granted Mr. Waugh to sell at the beerhothe known as the Volunteer Inn, Gran- vile-st., Runcorn. DOG OWNERS FINED.—The following persons were fined ss. including costs for allowing their dogs to be at large unmuzzled :—Peter Noon, Church-st. ; Arthur Lewis, 26, Church-st. ; Samuel Wright, railway porter, Norton ;and George Cobb, Heath-road, Weston. A MAINTENANCE ORDER.—Martin Gilligan, lodging- house keeper, Friar-st., was summoned to show cause why a maintenance order should tuit be made against him for his son whe was sent by the magistrates to an industrial school.—Superinterhiert Atherton asked for 2s. 6d. per week to be levied.—Defendant stated that he could not pay 2s. 6d. a week. He produced a doctor's certificate of ill-health, and stated that trade had been so bad that he had been obliged to pawn several of his things. He offered to pay a shilling per week, but the magistrates fixed the sum at la. 6d. and ordered the de- fendant to pay the costs, 93. 6d. ILLTEEATMENT OF A HORSE.—Peter Beckett, a boat- man of Barnton, was summoned for illtreating a horse by working it in an unfit state on July 19th. Evidence for the prosecution was given by Charles Pownall,cashier for Messrs. Simpson Davies, and Scns, who stated that the defendant had worked for them some time. On May 3rd, witness gave the defendant a horse to work with, belonging to the firm. It was then in a very good condition. He saw the animal again on July 19th, and it was suffering from a wound on the shoulder, and was in a very law condition from want of food. They re- ported the matter t the Inspector. The firm bought the horses and loaned them out to the boatmen. In answer to Inspector puff, R.S.P.C.A., witness stated that they had received complaints about the condition of the horse.—Edward Tucker, corn merehant,Runcorn, deposed that he saw the animal in question when it was turned out with the defendant on May 3rd. It was then in good condition but when brought back en July 19th, drawing a canal boat, it was suffer- ing from a wound on the shoulder,and was also in a very weak condition through being improperiy fed.—lnspec- tor Lull stated that he had examined the horse. It was very weak and unfit for work. There was a raw wound on the shoulder. Superintendent Atherton accompanied him to the stable.—Che defendant said the horse was not in good condition when he took it, and the wound was caused by the very poor collar the firm supplied.— The magistrates imposed a fine of 53. and costs, or in default seven days' imprisonment. He went to prison. A MIcCHIEVOUS YOUTH.—James Connor, 13 years of age, of Robert-street, Runcorn was summoned for un- lawfully destroying a quantity of growing p -itatoes in a field belonging to John Williamson, and doing damage to the extent of 2s.—John Williamson,jun., deposed that on August 9th he caught the defendant and another boy pulling up potatoes in his (witness's) father's field in Robert-street. He caught him once before.—The magis- trates ordered the defendant to pay the costs and ad- monished him. AN UNLICENSED HAWKER. —David Godfrey, who stated that he was a chemical worker of St. Helens, was chared with acting as pedlar without a certificate.—P.C. Butler caught the prisoner hawking boot laces from door to door in 80-Ali-street on Saturday night. On beinr, asked for his certificate he said he had none.— 1 I Fined ss. and cost or seven days' imprisonment. He chose the latter.

div.head: THE- MOON.
div.p: THE- MOON.

Hail, lovely moon, night's ruler thou ! MajNitic on thy peerless throne, 'Tis thine to reign supremely now. While heaven and earth thy sceptre own. No other power may claim thy seat No gsirish orbs around thee blaze: And nkture, resting at thy feet, In silence her devotion pays. When burnished with thy mystic beams The far off sky looks wondrous fair: Nor less the lonely landscape seems The lustre of those beams to share. Perchance some fitful clouds may hide Thy presence from the gazer's view: . But swiftly these are brushed aside Before thy glory bursting through. In every land, in every place, What loving eyes are turned to thine ! While wond'ring science scans thy face Where mysery lies in every line. Eternal change is written clear On all creation's work below: But no mutations mark thy sphere, No change thy phases ever know. Bright was thy smile on Eden's bowers When man was in his happy prima; And still, in night's long dreary hours, That smile is seen in every clime. Through all his wand'rings thou hast been A luridly watcher o'er his way ; And 0, thy gentle eyes have seen Bow frail he is and prone to stray. Shine on, 0 Moon with glory mild, His changeless friend, companion be ; Still guide him in the pathless wild, And cheer him on the lonely sea. J. 11. W. CLINDINNING.
