WARRINGTON v. SEFTON.—SENSATIONAL BOWLING . The majority of spectators who assembled at the Arpley enclosure on Saturday were hardly prepared for the sensational cricket which the afternoon's sport provided. The general opinion prevailed that small scoring would be the order, but no one was prepared to see Sefton dis- missed twice in one afternoon for the small aggregate of 74 runs. The fast drying wicket gave the bowlers every assistance, and a record was established for the Arpley enclosure in a first-class wicket, when Dr. R. Smith, the Warrington captain, succeeded in the second innings of the visitors in taking four wickets with successive ball, and had the remarkable analysis at one time of having six wickets for but a single run. Mr. Smith's record for the afternoon must stand out as one of the best achievements this season, and during the afternoon his record read as follows :-20 °vers, eight maidens, 18 runs, and twelve wickets. He was heartily applauded at the close of the afternoon's play, and his success did not end with his deadly attacks, for when Warrington went in a second time to get the 23 runs, the home cep. tam hit out with such vigour that 32 runs were chronicled in twenty minutes, the play winding up with a brilliant drive for six, clean out of the enclosure. The fielding was smart on both sides, whilst the wicket keeping of Clark was of the usual high order. Every- thing, however, pales before the performance of Mr. Smith, who will remember the return match with Sefton in 1895 as one of his most remarkable perform- ances. When Hampson appeared to be nicely set he was given out caught off his pads, a decision not giving general satisfaction. div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
FRIDAY.

In the House of ComniOn-s—o—nFriday evening Mr. W. I LONG, replying to questions, said he was still compelled to maintain in force the requirement that Canadian cattle should be slaughtered at the port ot landing. Answering Mr. Lonax, Sir M. W. RIDLEY said no means existed of stopping the publication of pernicious erature unless it was of an obscene, blasphemous or reditious character. Mr. BALFOUR informed Mr. LEWIS that he would con- sult with the Chairman of the Committee on the Unem- ployed which recently sat and see whether, in his opinion, any good would be served by reappointing the Committee.

In explaining to Mr. T. BOWLES the custom in regard to directorships which might be held by Ministers, the right hon. gentleman said he understood that a large number of the directorships held by members of the Government had been, and more were to be, resigned. Mr. CnANNtrto asked whether the Government pro- posed to take immediate steps to institute further in- quiry into the various schemes for making provision for the aged poor. Mr. BALFOUR said the Government were in favour of further investigation, and the subject was under consideration. _
A bill was brought in by Mr. T. M. HEALY and read a first time to amend the law relating to the municipal franchise in Ireland. _ _ _ _

The debate on the Address of Mr. J. REDMOND'S amendment thereto calling for a declaration of the Government's Irish policy and Mr. Datotes amend- ment calling upon the Government to legislate immedi- ately for the reinstatement of the Irish evicted tenants, was resumed. On the House dividing, Mr. DlLLoises amendment was rejected by 257 to 123 and Mr. RED,- MOND'S by 243 to 113.

Mr. CLasicv moved an amendment declaring that a time had come for a reconsideration of the case of the Irish treason-felony convicts. Sir M. W. RIDLEY said he cwt in ti-nrninA accord with the principles which guided the late Governmen in the action they took in this matter. He had no doubt that the decision of his predecessor was the right one. But he had not himself inquired into the cases, and he was prepared to apply to them the principles which regulated the conduct of the Home Office in regard to long sentences. He would reconsider the cases simply because he felt it his duty to satisfy himself that his responsibility was clear. But there was no political reason why the Government ought to consider any question of general amnesty, and if the amendment was pressed the Government must vote against it. Mr. J. REDMOND thought that under the circumstances nothing would be gained by pressing the amendment to a division. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said the cases of these men would be considered on nothing more or less than the rigid and inflexible rules applied to all such cases. Mr. Ascot= expressed his satisfac- tion with the language of the leader of the House. Mr. CLANCY withdrew his amendment.

Mr. PRICE moved an amendment drawing attention to the depression in agriculture, and calling for remedial measures in an autumn session in the present year. Mr. BROADHURST seconded the amendment. Mr. LNG de- clared the readiness of the Government to bring for- ward measures to relieve agriculture, " but not this ses- sion nor in an autumn session." The debate was ad- journed at midnight on the motion of Mr. CHANNINo.

div.head: MONDAY.-THE NEW COMMANDER IN
div.p: MONDAY.-THE NEW COMMANDER IN

In the House of Commons on Monday Sir M. W. RIDLEY, in answer to a question put by Mr. IsaacsoN, said that however foolish and degrading parachute descents might be, there was no pawer to interfere with them so far as adults were concerned. Mr. J. REDMOND asked whether the motion to be pro- posed by the FIRST LORD of the TREASURY with regard to the business of the House would preclude him from introducing a bill re-enacting the 13th clause of the Land Act of 1891, dealing with evicted tenants ; and if so, whether an exception could be made in favour of that bill. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR replied that it would be extremely inconvenient to make the exception, but he saw no objection to the Government themselves bringing forward the 13th section in the farm of a bill, it being understood that that would not be done until the Appro- priation Bill was reached, and that the bill should be accepted without discussion. On these conditions, he promised that the Government would introduce such a bill. _ _

_ Mr. BRODERICK Stated, in reply to Mr. SWIFT MacNEILL, that the name of the successor to the Duke of CAMBRIDGE would be announced before the Army Estimates were discussed. Mr. MacNEILL pressed for further information, and Mr. BRODRICK then said th It when the Dllif9 of CAMBRIDGE relinquished the command of the army Lord WOLRELEY would assume chief command. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR afterwards moved his resolution appropriatina all the time of the House for the rest of the session for Government business. After several amendments had been disposed of,. further divi- sion took place on Mr. BALFOUR'S original motion,which was carried by 248 votes to 100.

In the House of Lords on Monday the Marquis of LANSDOWNE, in answer to a question put by Lord MONKSWELL, said he was in a position to say that the Duke of CAMBRIDGE would relinquish the chief command of the army, not on the Ist of October as was originally proposed, but on the Ist November. When the Duke of CAMBRIDGE relinquished his p-ist of Commander-in-Chief he would be followed by Viscount WOLBELEY.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday Sir W. H. HOULDSWORTH asked if the Government would be favourable to the appointment of a Select Committee to consider the laws relating to the licensing and control of the liquoltraffin with a view to their amendment. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR replied that it would be impossible that such a Committee could be appointed during the present session to do any effective work. The question would, however, be considered by the Government dur- ing the recess. The ATTORNEY GENERAL moved a resolution declaring that JOHN DALY, having been sentenced to penal servi- tude for life for felony, was incapable of being returned as a member of the House. Mr. FIARRINGTON pointed out that the Election Petitions Act of 1868 referred to the 'question of inquiring into the returns to writs to a special ttibunal of judges,and the question was whether thellouse was competent to exercise jurisdiction in the same matter. He moved as an amendment that a Select Committee should be appoieted to examine into the pre- cedents and the law of Parliament. The amendment was rejected by 281 votes to 85. and the original resolutinn was passed by 256 votes to 74. Mr. T. M. HEALY asked how long the Government intended to allow Limerick to remain unrepresented as at present. Mr.A. J. BALFOUR said he thought the reotion for the issue of a writ rested with the party to which Daly belonged.
WEDNESDAY. THE SLAVE TRADE.

The House of Commons on Wednesday resumed the consideration of the Civil Service Estimates. On the vote for salaries and expenses in connection with the Foreign Office, Sir C. Unarm daked for information with regard to the position of affairs in Siam. He also con- demned the continued occupation of Egypt, and urged that the Government ought to take steps to bring slavery at Zanzibar to an end. Mr. H. M. STANLEY urged that the construction of a railway to Uganda was the key to the Egyptian problem. Mr. Curtzosi,in replying, stated that with regard to the general policy of the Government on the subject of the " buffer" State on the Mekong it was impbssible for him to say anything more at present. The Government were doing their best to grapple with the question of slave trading at Zanzibar. As to the evacuation of Egypt, the Government had assented to and would continue the pylicy that was pursued by the late Government. In the opinion of the Government the conditions under which evacuation would be possible had not beea ful- filled, nor had the time arrived for the reconsideration of the subkot. Mr. FLYNN moved the reduction of the vote by £l.OOO on the ground that satisfactory assur- ACERB had not been given in regard to the suppression of I slavery in the islands of Pemba and Zanzibar. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said the constructio, of a railway to Uganda would he one of the greatest steps that could be taken towards stamping out the slave trade, and the Govern- ment were pressing on the railway as quickly as pos- sible. The amendment was withdrawn, and the Tote was agreed to.

div.head: PRISONERS COMMITTED TO THE WAR' ER
div.p: PRISONERS COMMITTED TO THE WAR' ER
SESSIONS.

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Tuesday,l Joseph Brookes, shoemaker, Tilley-st., and James Gould- ing, fustian cutter, Halifax-st., were charged on remand with unlawfully cutting and wounding Thomas Fahey, at Orford, at 3 30 on Sunday afternoon, August 11. Thomas Fahey, farm labourer, Green Farm, Orford, said that on Sunday, August 11th, in the afternoon, he was returning home from Warrington with two mates, John Rafferty and John Shaughnessy, when they met Brookes and Goulding in a cinder lane, near Orford Hall. Brookes and Shaughnessy shouldered each other, upon which Brookes turned round and asked Shaughnessy if he was fond of shouldering. rhe latter replied that he could not help it. Brookes then pulled his coat off and threw it on the ground. Goulding then struck at Shaugh- nessy but missed him. Witness and his mates then walked on and Brookes went back to his coat and pulled out his knife. Rafferty and Shaughnessy ran away when they saw this,and shouted something which witness could not hear and walked on. Brookes run after them, and when be caught up to witness he lifted up his right hand and attempted to at icy him on the head. Witness raised his hand to ward off the blow,and received a severe stab on the wrist. Rafferty then came back as he saw blood coming from a large cut. Witness had a knife in his pocket but he did not have it in his hand. A hand- kerchief was put round the wound, and the three then went to Dr. Hall's surgery in Winwick-st.,where the arm was dressed. The prisoners walked in front of them for about a hundred yards. Witness's hat was knocked off in the lane,but he could not say who knocked it off. Raf- ferty found a hat all cut up. Witness did not know the prisoners and had not had any quarrel with them. John Shaughnessey, farm labourer, residing at Kill- shaw's farm, Burtonwood, said that on the 11th August, about 3.15, Thomas Fahey, himself, and a man named John Rafferty were walkiug towards Orford when they met Brookes and Goulding. He (witness) by accident knocked up against Brookes, who then asked him to fight, at the same time pulling off his coat and placing it on the ground. Goulding then rushed at him (witness) and struck him on the chest. After a short quarrel Brookes shouted "I will soon settle them." He (Brookes) then went to his coat and took a knife from one of the pockets, and rushed at Fahey. He then made a thrust I at Fahey's head, but he put up his arm to stop the blow, thus receiving the blow on the wrist. Prisoners then walked away, and were followed by two or three men who were near. He (witness) went with Fahey to Dr. Hall's surgery, where the wound was dressed. John Rafferty,farm labourer,residing at Green's farm, Orford, corroborated the last witness's statement. I Frank Singleton, of Houghton Green, and Henry ICliffe, engine driver, and living at 40, Gee-st., gave cor- roborative evidence.

P.C. Johnson, of the County Constabulary, stated that he received news of the affair from Constaole Chrimes on the Sunday night. Ile then accompanied him to War- rington. where at midnight they arrested Brookes. Great difficulty was experienced in doing this, as the prisoner got on to the house top, and was running and pimping about like a madman. It took about twelve constables to affect his arrest.

The magistrates remarked that Brookes had a very bad record, and the two prisoners would be committed to take their trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions,bail being allowed to Goulding in a sum amounting to £4O. The case was very protracted and lasted about three hours and a half.

ST. MARY'S (R.C.) CHURCH, LATCHFORD The annual sermons in connection with the Sunday sc iota belonging to the above church were preached on Sunday, by the Very Rev. Father Alphonsus, D.D.0.5.F.C., of the Monastery, Chester. The congreg- ations were large, and the sermons were thoroughly appreciated. A special collection in aid of the Sunday schools was made at each service.

WYCLIFFE P.S.A.—QUARTERLY OPEN MEE C.ENG. On Sunday afternoon Wycliffe Congregation al Church was crowded, the occasion being the quarte-ly open meeting of the P.S.A. Society, and, as usual on this occasion, there was a plentiful sprinkling of ladies. Un- fortunately the first announcement which the Rev. J. Yonge, president, had to make, was that Mr. Chandos Wilson, who was expected to speak, was ill and unable to fulfil his engagements, Wycliffe included. As sub- stitute, however, the services of Mr. Telford, of Man- cheater, had been secured.

The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Bircball, J.P.,who, after scripture reading by Mr. G. Brown, and the sing- ing of a hymn, said he would have felt justified in send- ing an apology for non-attendance as he had scarcely any voice,but he had such a strong desire to come,that notwithstanding that fact he thought he would be present that afternoon for the first time at one of the open meetings. He had often been struck with the beautiful motto of the Association " Brief, Bright, and Brotherly," and as to its briefness he had thought that he would have liked it to go on longer at times ; its brightness he had felt in being sent back from the meet- ings more cheerful than before and with a feeling that he had spent an hour pleasantly and profitably,and then as to its brotherliness—the fact that they had kept it together in the years since it was formed, he was sure was a testimony of its brotherliness. (Applause.) He was pleased to see that it had not only taken hold of the male portion but also interested their wives and sisters, and perhaps also some tenderer relations, (laughter and applause). The speaker had no doubt that some of the brightness there was carried to the homes of the mem- bers and to those whom they loved.lt was a curious char- acteristic of many Englishmen that at hone they were very often the dullest and did not wear their hearts upon their sleeves, and seemed to think that they should not show too much affection or interest in things going on at home. They ought to be there at their best, and with the gift of speech they could make it much better if they tried. He had great faith in what a Britisher could do if be set to work to do it. (Applause.) _

Mr. r 'earnest and somewhat humorous address, which was listened to with pleasure by his hearers. The brightness and attraction of the meeting was very greatly increased by the hi2hly effi:ient cornet solos rendered by Mr. R. Pierpoint of Runcorn. Mr. Yonge announced at the close, that in order to largely augment the membership in the coming new year of the association,they had decided upon a system of house-to-house visitation by the members, whom he there and then exhorted to give their energies to this scheme.

div.head: CROWN AND THE ARMY.
div.p: THE CROWN AND THE ARMY.

The announcement that the successor of the Duke of Cambridge in the post of commander-in-chief of the army is to be an officer who is not the prince of the blood may says the " Westminster Gazette," render of interest some circumstances connected with the interest of this office. Sir Theodore Martin in his "Life of the Prince Con- sort," states that "at this early period (1842) the ap- pointment of commander-in-chief in the event of the de- mise of the Duke of Wellington had been privately con- templated by the Ministry, and was even discussed between Lord Aberdeen and B4ron Stockmar. From him, however, it received no encouragement. On the I contrary, he at once expressed his decided disapproval of the project" (" Life of the Prince Consort," 1., p. 150). Again, in March, 1845, the Prince Consort relates, in a letter to Baron Stockmar that he had discussed with ' Sir Robert Peel, who was then Prime Minister, tho ques- tion of the commander-in-chief, and that Sir Robert Peel had said in regard to the commander-in-chief" that the army would be greatly pleased by ittthat politically it would be the beat arrangement " (" Life of the Prince Consort," 1., p. 259). In a letter, however, written by the Duke ot Wellington in April 1850, when a similar proposal had been made, the Prince entered at length into his close relationship with the occupant of the throne, and asks, 't How far would it be consistent with this position to undertake the management and admini- stration of a most important branch of the public ser- vice and the individual responsibility attaching to it— becoming an executive officer of the Crown, receiving the Sovereign's commands through her Secretaries of State, &c.? " ("Life of the Prince Consort, IL, p. 260.) The sound discretion of the Prince Consprt in refusing this appointment by reason of his position was demonstrated some years later in December, 1855. The Prince,as occupying a position very subordinate to that of commander-in-chief, and, in fact,almost purely honorary, that of colonel of the Grenadier Guards, was placed in a false position with reference to the Crown and the country. The officers of the Grenadier Guards memorialised the Queen for the purpose of obtaining redress for an alleged grievance, by which, owine to the operation of a royal warrant, lieutenant colonels, after three years' service in actual command of a battalion, became by right full colonels of officers of the line, but not if they were officers of the Guards. The prince, as colonel of the Grenadier Guards, had appended his name to the memorial,, whereupon he was attacked by the "Times," which madernention of "a general assertion that the Prince exercised much influence in military matters, especially as respects the highest military appointments," and said that it was intolerabl( that the Queen should be placed in the ungracious position of rof using the prayer of one who ought to be careful how be sues when he should not sue in vain, since his signature "almost converted " the'prayer of the petition into "a command " (" Life of the Prince Consort." 111., p. 412). Mr. Gladstone thus comments on the contem- plated appointment of the Prince Consort to the com- mandership-in-chief :

"Everyone acquainted with the spirit ofParliamentary Government must at once have seen it to be indefensible or in a high degree inconvenient. It is, indeed, to be desired that a very close relation of sentiment between the Sovereign and the army should be permanently maintained. But the army is, after all, a great department of State, and the departments of the State can only be administered in this country by persons responsmlo to Parliament. Tho Prince could not fulfil the very first among the conditions of fitness for the office: he could not be removable Years," 1., p. 345. (" Gleanings of Past

ATHLETICS.

CRICXST. The W arringtonians continue to go strongly and ,thanks chiefly to their bowling and fielding, they are basing revenge upon those woo beat them earlier in the season. Their record this season is in striking contrast with last season's results, and it is a remarkable circumstance that as team has been able to beat them ';wice, nor as they have only four more fixtures on the card, will any team Mai them twice. By their victory over Sefton on Satur- day, they counterbalanced the opening game of the season. They have beaten and been beaten by Preston. With Manchester, 0 dham and Northern they have won a match and drawn one. They have lost and abandoned a mateh with Broughton; with Liverpool, they have lost and drawn one, while they have only yet had one match each with Wigan and Little Lever which they have won, and one with Bolton which they drew. Ihere is, there- fore, every prospect of a good record at the close of the Season, despite the bad beginning.

_ Two innings were played with Sefton on Saturday, and Warrington won by six wickets and four runs. The match was remarkable for the lowness of scoring on each side. In fact, in the first innings of both Sefton and Warrington, not a single batsman obtained double ligures. The batting improved a little in the second innings, for Rogers. Collins and Oakley obtained 10, 10 and 11 respectively for Sefton, while R. Smith scored 21 not out. The Seftonians in their first innings were dis- missed for 26, which is the lowest score ever made by

div.head: them.
div.p: them.

The hero of the match was the home skipper. Dr. Smith was almost unplayable with the ball, and at one time, he bowled four men in four successive balls, and his record in the second innings was seven wickets for eight runs, and in the two innings, he took 12 wickets tor 18 runs. He was also the top scorer of the match, so that he has every reason to be satisfied with himself. J. J. Crosfield had a good analysis in the first innings tak- ing four wickets for 14 runs, but this was spoiled in the second venture, when his solitary wicket cost 38 runs. Bates could scarcely have done better than he did with the chance he got, for he sent down two balls, the first was blocked, and the second took the last Sefton wicket, so that he had one wicket for no runs. It is usual to call the feat of taking three wickets with three successive balls, the " hat" trick, but Smith took four, and this is so rare an occurrence that it has not yet obtained a name. Warrington' and Smith in particular, has every reason to be satisfied with their performance against Sefton.
-S-aCuida;

The lowness of the scores on Saturday, has had its effect upon the averages this week, only Smith among the "top sawyers" raising his average, and he now deposes J. J. Crosfield for the top place. He has also passed his third century of runs,and is actually 92 ahead of the next, in the list. H. Hind lost first place last week, and he has now got to the fourth. Clark and Bates are still together, but the wicket keeper now heads the senior professional. There is, however, not very much change in the positions of the players, and the following is the table this week : times

innings not out runs average B. Smith .. . ........ 13 ......... 1 J. J Croatia'. Lieu. Plomer 8 H Hind Clark (A) Bates W M Podmore ... 11 ......... 2 E England 8 ......... 2 ......... 64 J Callon W Mortimer 7 0 GClarke WWordsworth ... 6 lii Woods E Connor Lieu. Tupman 4 ----

The Warrington second team were easy victims to Sefton second, and at one period of the match it ap- peared as though the Seftonians' majority would have been even greater than three wickets and 104 runs, for at the commencement of the Warrington innings, three wickets fell for only one run, and that an extra. The remaining batsmen, however, shaped a little better, and 71 was obtained. Bibby and Silccck scoring 16 each, and Unsworth 10 not out. The fielding of the Warring- ton men was not of a very high order, in fact it was slovenly and a good number of " catches "were missed.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL.

An ordinary monthly meeting of the above Council was held in Mr. Sutton's Chambers,Bewsey-st., on Wed. nesdaq afternoon, the Rev. G. F. Roberts presiding There were also present Messrs. William Hon ghton. J. Di,gnum, J. W. Knowles. T. Halton. J. H oughton, and J. Ball ; also Mr. S. Sutton (clerk), Mr. F. Ker- toot (nuisance inspector),Mr. William Owen (surveyor). and Dr. Sephton. (medical officer). RH-APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS. The Cr. Eat, after reading the accounts for the past month, read a letter from the Local Government Board sanctioning the re-anpointment of Dr.Sephton as medical officer for June 189li and June 1896, at a salary of £100; also the re-appointment of Mr. F. Kerfoot as nuisance inspector at an increased salary of £llO. Tar .IS.ROOK AT FENKETH. Correspondence was read from Captain Hughes' agent with reference to the diverting of the sewage from Pen- keth breok through a sewer which the Council proposed to cut through his land, and which stated that Captain Hughes was prep ired to grant permission for this on 24;W:a of RI per annum. Mr. tudt,iuli. reCoMmended that this be allowed,and Mr. Halton having seconded, the motion was carried. In the Nuisance Inspector's report was a complaint that the brook had overflowed its banks and filled a tank at Penketh Hall, owing to there being a flood and high tide at the same tint.-1b was decided t'.; Ditchfield increase the height of the bank of the brook with clay and charge the Council. A DANGEROUS BRIDGE AT COLLINS GREEN. A letter was read from toe clerk to the Bortonwood Parish Council dat-d August Ist, stating that he was directed to ask for one or two lamps to be put under the Railway Bridge at Collins Gree.u, which Was dark and dangerous. He also directed the Council's attention to the water supply of Mr. Whitfield's cottages at Col- lins Green, complaints having been made as to its inade- quacy. After some discussion it was decided that the Parish Council be met and the questions considered. The CLERK reported that the audit of accounts was finished and that the auditor reported favourably upon them.

THE SURVEYOR'S REPORT. Mr.Owm,the surveyor reported that the drains of the houses belonging to the Colliery Company, at Collins Green, were well in hand and nearly ready for connec- tion to the main sewer, so that arrangements would shortly have to he made to deal with the sewage at the altering tanks. Rs also reported that the streets off Liverpool-road, Sankey Bridges were now ready to be handed over to the Highway Board.

div.head: PADdATE.
div.p: PADdATE.

TRIP FROM PAIDGATE. A trip to Southport was held on Saturday for the children attending the Padgate Wesleyan Band of Hope. Quarter-Master Sergeant Mantle and Mr. Henry Ward, the leaders of the Temperance Society were in charge of the arrangements. The party, to the number of 48, assembled at the Padgate Railway Station about 030 a.m.. where special carriages were in waiting. These %fere attached to the ordin- ary train to Southport, that place being reached about 10.45. The children were allowed to enjoy themselves as they pleased, and various ways were found in which to do this. Dinner was provided at the Temperance Institute, and was greatly relished. It was arranged that the party should meet at the station at 6.45 p m., and when the roll was called at this time everyone was found to be present. Padgate was reached about nine o'clock. Messrs. Mantle and Ward are to be complimented upon the excellent arrangements they had made.

the death at Cologne on the 14th inst. is announced of Sir George Martin-Holloway, of Tittenhurst, Sunt- bill, Berkshire. The deceased knight, who was in his 62nd year, was married to the sister of the late Mrs. Thomas Holloway. of 78, New Oxford-st. He was a man of considerable culture, fine physigoe. and many social qualities. He will be, perhaps, best known for his work in connection with the completion of the schemes for the Holloway Sanatoriurn,opened by H.R.FI. the Prince of Wales in 1885,and the Royal Holloway Col- lege, opened by her Majesty the Queen in June 1886,f0r 'which he received the honour of knighthood. He was governor and trustee of both these institutions,and dur- ing the last ten years of his life was intimately con- nected with their working. In addition to his duties in the management of Holloway's eminently successfisl patent medicine business,in partnership with his brother- in-law, Mr. Driver Holloway, Sir George was an active member of the Red Cross Society, and a Past Master of the Youlterers' Company, in the workings Of which he took considerable interest, having presented to the latter during the year that he filed the post of Master, two handsome, massive, loving cups.

div.head: EA.RLESTOWN A.ND N EWTON.
div.p: EA.RLESTOWN A.ND N EWTON.
VIADITCT INSTITUTE TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSES.

In connection with the elementary shorthand class held at the Institute for the session 1894-5, the following students havetbeen awarded certific- ates by the teacher (Mr. R. King) for having made good progress during the session named :-11. Beresford, E. H. Cotterill, J. W. Gilmour, L Harvey, Marion Holt, Mary Longworth, M. F. McCawley, R. W. Nicholson, C. Spencer and C E. Wright. 1.0.G.T. EARLESTOWN EBENEZER LODGE. This lodge held its weekly session on Tuesday one member being admitted to membership. Bro. W. J. Taylor read a circular from the District Lodge and Bro. A. Morris gave a report of the District Lodge Council, a slight decrease in juveniles being reported. The programme was afterwards pro- ceeded with. The following taking part : Sisters Taylor, Woods, Hall, Brown, and Broster ; and Bros. Brown, Morris, J. Taylor, Dean, Hatton, Hall and others, the Lodge closing after a very successful programme. ACCIDENT TO A CHILD.—NARROW ESCAPE. On Tuesday a little girl named Crosby, 18 months old, daughter of James Crosby,Legh-st.,Earlestown, had a marvellous escape from death by being run over. The child was playing with other children in the street near her home, Mr.liowarth, milkman,at the time delivering milk from his float. It is sup- posed the child must have been near the wheel when the horse was started, and been knocked down,or she fell just as the float mcved,but whatever the cause the wheel grazed the back of her head, causing an ugly abrasion, from which the blood flowed freely. The child was taken to Dr. Mounsey who dressed the wound,and she is now progressing favourably. EARLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODISTS. Special services in connection with the anniver- sary of the chapel were held in the above place of worship on Sunday. The preacher for the day was , the Rev. D. T. Maylott, of Walkden, who delivered , forcible addresses to large congregations present on each occasion. In th a afternoon a service of sacred song, entitled "Jack the sea waif " was excellently rendered by the chapel choir, and was evidently much enjoyed by the large audience present. The principal solos were taken by Misses Stronach, Dickens, L. Dickens, Mrs. Rawlings, and Master A. Banton. The connective readings were fluently given by Mrs. Smith, and Mr. Banton, in the absence of Mr. Dickens, conducted. The collec- tions were in aid of the reduction of the chap& debt.

GOOD TEMPLARY. The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars was held at the Co-opera- tive Hall on Monday evening, when there was a fair attendence of members. Bro. J. Hatton, CT., presided, and there were present as visitors, Bro. Sergeant Roberts. C.C.T., Warrington, and Bro. Westerling of Prescot, One candidate was admitted to membership. Bro. E. Newman, S.J.T., gave a report of the quarterly meeting of the juvenile council held at St. Helens on Saturday. The lodge was then declared open, and a good number of friends were admitted. Bro. G. E. Warburton and G. Clarke were responsible for the programme, and the former presided. After the opening ode the Chairman gave a short address, and an interesting programme of songs, readings, and recitations was given, the following taking part. Sisters Willis, Warburton, R. Warburton, Bros. Willis, Hopkins, J. Taylor, and G.Clarke. Bros. Westerling and Clarke delivered short addresses which brought an in- teresting session to a close. EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. The 139th quarterly meeting of the above Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Mr. J. Moss presided, but there was not a large muster of members. The report and statement of accounts which was for 12 weeks only, showed that the casti receipts for goods sold amounted to £3,658 34, 7d. The net profit for divi- sion amounted to £516 94. 7f1., which allowed of a dividend of 2s. 10d. in the .0 to members and is. 51 in the pound to non-members, leaving a balance of £l4 to he carried forward as a dividend reserve,and .£1 3s. 101-1. to the Contingent fund. During the quarter nine new members had been admitted, and 25 had withdrawn or been struck off, leaving 991 on the books. The average purchases ot these amount to £6 for the 12 weeks, or 108. per week. 'I he average on the whole of those on the books amounted to ▪ I7s. Olt or 6s. 51 per week. The balance sheet after a lengthy discussion was generally considered satisfactory. and was adopted. Messrs. D. Forrester and T. Holliday were elected to serve on the Com- mittee of Management. Mr. J. Gooding was reappointed auditor. This was all the business. MARRIAGE OF MISS JACKSON. On Wednesday afternoon at St. John's Church, Earlestown, Miss Lilian Maud Jackson, eldest daughter of Mr. Thomas Jackson. co!liery salesman, of Cross-lane, Earlestown, was united in marriage to Mr. J. T. Lomax of Preston. Tee officiating minister was the Rev. T. R. Matthews, and the bride, who was attired in a cream crepon dress, with tulle veil, and wreath of real orange blossoms, was given away by her father. Her bridesmaid-8 were Miss Patten (Widnes), cousin to the bride, Miss Effie Jackson (sister), and the Misses Obersby of Liverpool. The two former wore green crepon dresses with pink silk bodices and black velvet picture hats, and the latter wore pale pink dre,ses. After Ole Ceremony a reunion was held in one of the rriZ,tna of the Town Han nu 71.110 there were donut 40 guests, and the festivitiea were kept, UP until late in the evening. During the afternoon the newly married couple left for Scotland where the honeymoon will be spent. There was a large number of useful and costly presents WORKPROPLE'S TRIP FROM NEWTON. , On Saturday the annual excursion in connection with the printing works of Messrs. McCorquodale and Co., of Newton took place. This execursion by reason of the low rates at which the public are al- lowed to travel, is eagerly looke 1 forward to, and has now become quite a popular event.As in former years two places were fixed upon, viz.. Liverpool and IllackpooLthe majority selecting for their day's outing, the popular Lancashire seaport resort. Shortly after seven o'clock two trains carrying about 1,100 people left, Newton and reached Black- pool about nine o'clock. An hour later the train conveyed 600 more to Liverpool, and the day being exceptionally fine, tthe trip to each place was thoroughly enjoyed. of course those who chose Liverpool extended their wanderings and after a short sail on one of the ferry boats invaded Cheshire, chiefly round about New Brighton*. The Liverpool train returned home in good time, but last, train from Blackpool aid not reach Earlestown until after one o'clock on Sunday morning. THE LATE COLONEL MCConquoDaLE. At a meeting of the Earlestown Viaduct Institute Technical Instruction Committee held last week, Mr. J. W. Emmett nresiding, and there being pre- sent Messrs. C. B. F. Borron, J.P., C.C., C. W. Em- mett, F. J. Wood, W. Thompson, junr., W. Craw- ford, W. Davies, and T. Ormand, secretary, the following resolution was unanimously passed,before the usual business was proceeded with, on the motion of the Chairman "That it is with very sincere regret we have to record the death of one of our oldest and largest prize clamors, in the person of Colonel McCorquodale. It is now nearly 17 years since he first stimulated and aided educational pro- gress in connection with thislnstitute by promising the handsome donation of £5 per annum to be coin • peted for bN the youths employed at the printing i works, Newton-le-Willows, and at the wagon works. rarlestown, subsequently thrown open to the whole of the students in the district of Newton in Makerfield ; and further, this Committee desires to give expression to its appreciation of the late , Colonel McCorquodale'a universal kindness and large heartedness and begs to assure Mrs. McCor- quodale and her family of its deepest sympathy in the great loss they have sustained," The resolution was seconded by Mr. Thompson. and the Secretary was instructed to forward a copy to Mrs. McCor- quodale and her family.

div.head: MINERS' DEMONSTRATION AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: MINERS' DEMONSTRATION AT HAYDOCK.
SIR CHARLES DIGICE ON LABOUR REPRE- SENTATION. MR. S. WOODS ON THE RECENT ELECTION.

Under the auspices of the Ashton, Haydock, Bolton Seo., Miners' Trade Union, a grand demonstration of the Elaydock, Ashton and Bamfurlong miners took place on Saturday, in Hayeleck Park, by the kind permission of Councillor C. H. Astle. The various lodges and miners' associations met at Ashton at one o'clock, and marched in procession, to the number of 6,000, to Haydock Park. Here a platform had been erected, and an open-air meeting was held, the principal speakers being Sir Charles Dilke,M.P. (who had come down specially from London), and Mr. Sam Woods. Mr. John Burns, M.P., was expected to be present, but was unable to attend owing to the illness of his wife. Councillor John Fors- ' ter (St. Ileens), presided, and in opening the proceed- ings said the South-West Lancashire federation was one of the strongest in the country, and he urged the men to stand true to their interests to persuade every miner to join it. The employers would respect them if they had a good organisation and were true to their cause and their leaders. (Cheers.) Mr. S. Walsh moved the following resolution :—"That we, the miners of Ashton, Haydock, and surrounding districts, in meeting assembled, hereby declare our ear- nest belief that the depression existing in British indus- tries is largely cansed by our inequitable land system, in consequence of which system mines have been and are being flooded with unskilled labour, to the great increase of danger in the mines and reduction of the miners' wages. This meeting is further of opinion that a serious evil and standing injustice exist in the system of fixed and royalty rents,whereby, although wages are lowered and profits impossible, the landower reaps the full bene- fit of the enterprise, and escapes his fair share of local taxation "(applause). Mr. T. Greenall (Pendlebury) seconded, and Messrs. Chadwick an Worthington having supported the reso- lution, it was carried with applause. Mr. Josiah Hayes (Ashton) then moved the following resolution, which was seconded by Mr. James Lawren- son, and supported by Mr. IV. E. Harvey (Derbyshire) : —" That we strongly condemn the system of private reductions which has of late years become so prevalent in the county of Lancaster, whereby the misery of the workman isencreased, trade disturbances fermented ,and good feeling between employer and workmen rendered impossible. We are further of opinion that peace could never be permanently established in the mining indus- try until the system of private reductions is abolished. The meeting is further of opinion that no Employers' Liability Bill can be considered satisfactory which con- tains any clause enabling the employers or workmen to contract out of its provisions, emphasises the necessity of the miners' eight hours' day, and appeals to all miners to rally round trades' unionism, so that these desirable objects may be attained ". (Applause). Sir Charles Dilke, M.P., in supporting the resolution, assured his hearers that he was a firm believer in the edventages of trades' unionism and the necessity of it to workers if they were to maintain the position they had won. There was little preepect Of (he Miners' Eight flours Bill in the present ParlJareeht, especially SO fa.r as Lancashire WM ConCiened, for it had lost ground at the last elretioD, The returns at the recent elections showed that the working people of Lancashire had separated themselves from the Liberal party as at present consti- tuted. They had, however, he thought, put the repre- sentation of the county too completely into the hands of one class. end had left them in Parliament no Lanca- shire miners, no Lancashire operatives,to represent their views, as in many c ises they could only be represented by men of their own class. Recently in discussions on the Factory Bill—as, for example, in the discussions on the cleaning of machinery by children, young persons, and women—they had found themselves wholly in the hands of the manufacturers, beeause there were none present who could speak with absolute authority in the name of the working people as to the evils which all of them, by means of written statements from those con- cerned, knew to exist. (Hear, hear.) There never was a parliament in which there was more need for such rep- resentation of the working people at Lancashire than the present. (Hear, hear.) Sir Charles called the atten- tion of the work,nen of the country belonging to all trades to the need of applying to the Secretary of State for the Home Department to put in force sub-section 6 of section 40 of the Factory Acteto as to extend to them the Lancashire "particulars clause," which had hitherto applied to textile industries only. (Cheers.) Mr. Sam Woods (late member of the Ince Division) also supported the resolution,and was accorded a hearty reception. In the course of his remarks he said he was ashamed of the representation of Lancashire in the pre- sent HOUSE, of Commons. It was a disgrace to Lan- cashire workingmen—(hear, bear)—and he hoped that by organisation and unanimity of action they would wipe out that disgrace at the earliest possible moment. (Applause.) From one end of the county to the other the men whom they had sent to the House of Commons were deadly enemies of labour and pregrees, and were against every measure that was calculated to improve their social, their moral, and their financial position. (Applause.) While in South \Vales the miners had re- turned Mr. Abrams, Northumberland and Durham, Messrs. Fenwick and Wilson, and Yorkshire Mr.Pickard, their erand old champion, by a triumphant majority the workingmen of Ince had turned him (Mr. Woods) out at tee three years'experience. (" Shame.") Had he stood in any other county than Lancashire, he believed the working classes never would for one moment have allowed him to be at the bottom of the poll—(cheers) and returned a man to represent them who was their inveterate enemy so far as their cam.e and true inter- ests were concerned. (Applause.) Ile was afraid that the result of the e'ection was one of the greatest blows that had ever been struck to labour during the last hell century. (Applause.) They were doomed, un- less some favourable dispensation of Provi- dence or some wholly unexpected incident occurred, to penal servitude for the next six or seven years. During that time workingmen would have time for reflection, and if it was not that the innocent had to suffer with the guilty, he should not regret the ordeal. (Applause, and a Voice : "Well done, Sam.") Contina- ice, Mr, Woods said he Was afraid the Miners' Eight Flours' Bill was doomed to oblivion as far as the present Government was concerned. He could not conceive how men weuld allow themselves to be bought and sold like dumb cattle in the market for the sake of a glass of beer,
or 5a., or the promise of a good place— trr 'tire mTh-nr as they had daring the late elections. They ought rather to give intelligent expression to their in- . ..

ward conviction;, and strike a bloc; for the freedom arid advancement of their cause. (Cheers.) Mr. Woods later on referred to the recent libel action in which he had beer, engaged as prosecutor, and said that the alle- gations made by the other side constituted a libel upon the trades' unions of this country,than which there W4P no body or organisation of any kind whose accounts were kept in a more straightforward, pure, honest, and just manner. (Applause.) In conclusion, the speaker said ho hoped the miners of Lancashire would begin to pull themselves together, for if any good was to coma to them arid to their families for the improvement of their future position, it would have to be done by every miner and workman making a long poll, a strong pull, and a pull altogether. (Loud applause ) On the motion of Mr. Vt alkden, seconded by Council- lor Turner, votes of thanks were accorded the various' speakers, after which the meeting concluded, the proceedings throughout being characterised by great enthusiasm.

div.head: WARRINGTON BREWSTER
div.p: WARRINGTON BREWSTER
SESSIONS.
FRESH APPLICATIONS REFUSED.

The annual Brewster Sessions for the borough of War- rington were held on Thursday morning at the Warring- ton Borough Police Court, but in striking contrast to last 3 ear, there was not much public interest,shown in them and the court did not present any unusual appearance. The following were the magistrates present, the Mayor (chairman), Alderman Sutton, Colonel Ridgway, Mr. John Fairclough, Mr. T. Birchall, Dr. Gornall, Alder- man Francomb, Alderman Wright, Mr. S. Wright, Mr. J. H. Fleming, Mr. R. Garnett, Councillor Roberts, Mr. J. Burgess, and Mr. J. W. Hayward.

THE OLD LICENSES RENEWED. The CHIEF CONSTABLE said that during the year, so far as the licensed victuallers were concerned, there had been no charges against them. With regard to the cif -Bemis( s there had been one case.

Mr. WHITE (magistrates' clerk) then asked whether there were any objections to any fully licensed house that morning. No objection being raised, Mr. White asked if there were any objections to any beer house license. There was also no reply to this. Mr. White then asked whether there were any objections to off- licenses.—The Mayor : There has only been one person fined who has kept an off-license.—Mr. Hunt: The ten- ant left the house a month or six weeks afterwards, and the license was transferred to another person against whom I have no objection. . There being no objections to any of the licenses, they were all renewed.

div.head: NSW APPLICATIONS.
div.p: NSW APPLICATIONS.

There were two new applications. Mr. Benjamin Kenyon applied for a wine license for the Green Man. and Mr. Benjamin Johnson for an off-license to sell in a provision shop at 70, Wellfield-street, off Mill-lane. These were heard before the Liceasing Committee, consisting of Like Mayor, and Messrs. J. Fairclough, J. H. Fleming, and J. W. Hayward. . .

Mr. Booms -I's said that he applied on behalf of Mr. Benjamin Johnson for an out-door license at 70, Well- field-street, at the corner of Percy-street, in the White- cross ward. This was a shop occupied by Mr. Johnson who for 15 years in the Potteries kept a fully licensed house without any complaint whatever from the police there, and who latterly kept the British Workman public-house at the corner of Milner-street, but was compelled for private reasons to leave that house and had since lived at his present premises. As to the character of the applicant, there could be no possible objection. He would like to remind the bench that the number of licenses had continued the same since 1878, although they all knew that the population had almost doubled itself. Moreover the portion of the Whitecross ward where the shop in question was situated was in a part which was formerly outside the borough and was added to the borough a year or tw• ago, and there were no less than 200 added houses put up there within the last few years The applicant did not intend to sell any provisions, and therefore there could not be any opportunity to put beer down for soap or groceries, and no harm could possibly be done.Further,in support of the application,he was go- ing to meet the so-called temperance people on their own ground. There were 318 houses in the immediate neigh- bourhood of the shop at the present time, of which 30 houses were empty. That would leave something like 290. He had a memorial in his hand which was signed , by occupiers only, in the presence ot a person whom he would call, and there were 150 signatures in support of ' the license. Therefore on the grounds of local option alone, he asked for that license to be granted. The nearest outdoor beer-house was Mr. Throssall's in Lovely lane, who had no objection. The nearest beerhouse was the Green Man, Sankey Green, and the nearest fully 1 licensed house was the Bowling Green Hotel, which was considerably over a quarter of a mile away. He con- tended that the applicant was clearly entitled to the license to sell beer off the premises. I BENJAMIN Johnson, the applicant, said that he lived lat 70 Wellfield-street,the house part being in Percy-street He paid 83. 6d. per week in rent, and the property be- longed to Mr. Davenport, builder, Stockton Heath. He had lived 12 years in Warrington, and had lived 15 I years at the Star and Garter,Kidsgrove,and no complaiat whatever had been made against his conduct in that house. He had latterly kept the British Workman public house at the corner of Milner-street. The nearest out- door beerhouso was Mr. Thressall's,which was 250 yards away. Mr. Allen's house was 400 yards away. Many houses had been built in the district of late, and at the present time, there were 28 other houses being erected. All the signatures produced were made in his presence, and the persons were in favour of the licence. Some of them had told him that if they had had time they would have been at the court that morn- ing to support the application. There was another license being applied for, but that had been dropped,and that had no doubt hindered him from getting more signatures than he had done. He had posted the notices as required by law. Mr. F. R. ROBERTS, MA., L.L. 8., said that he ap- peared on behalf of various ratepayers to object to the application. Mr. BROWER said that he wished to know who those ratepayers were. Mr. ROBERTS said that he would mention them if the Brh desired it. The MAYO 6 said that of course they would like to know who they were. Mr. ROBERTS replied that he appeared on behalf of Captain Savage, Wellfield-st.,Mr. Walter Brough,Lovely. lane, and others. Mr. ROBERTS then proceeded to cross-examine Mr. Johnson. In reply to questions as to how long he had been at the Milnee-st. British Workmen's public-house, he replied : For two years.—What was the reason of your leaving it ? Sickness.—Were you not dismissed ? I was partly. I partly left on my own accord. —That is very curious. You were partly dismissed, and partly left. Were you not dismissed ?—No. They spoke rather sharply to me.—Was there not a great deal of unplea- santness about the accounts ?—There was.—Did not you pay back a certain sum ?—I did pay it back. Mr. Baownk asked whether it was the British Work- man Public-house Co., who were objecting. Mr. ROBERTS said that he was questioning as to character.

ROBERT ISHERWOOD, Lovely-lane, was then called. He said that he was the agent for the shop in question, and had let it at 81. 61 per week. That was a fair sum for the locality, but if it was nearer the town it would be more valuable. There was a good shop, kitchen, par- lour, five bedrooms, and two cellars. He had lived in the neighbourhood a good number of years,and although he was a teetotaler he had no objection to the apelici- tion. There were 318 houses in the vicinity, and 86 bouses in Wellfield-st., occupied. James William Sullen, clerk to Mr. Browne, said that he had served notice of the application upon the assis- tant ()Veneer of the poor, and also upon the chief con- st Mr. -Roberts said he would reserve his remarks until the atpplication of Mr. Kenyon was heard. Benjamin Kenyon, who applied for a wine license for the Green Man, said that he had served the notices re- quired. The Green Man was owned icy his wife,and the rates amounted to £5O per annum.—Cross-examined by Mr. Roberts, he said that he had applied for a license before and had been refused. The Bowling Green Inn was not far Iron his house. If he got the license, he did not know whether he should apply in some future time for a spirit license. Mr. Roberts then addressed the Bench on behalf of the objectors. He said that as regarded the memorial, he thought it highly irregular. At all events,their Worships refused to receive memorials. Mr. Browne : But I have a witness ef the signatares in the present case. Mr. Roberts said that with regard to Mr. Johnson's application he thought that their worships would not be quite satisfied as to the character of the applicant, as it was not all that could be desired, and he admitted under cross-examination that he was partly dismissed and partly withdrew from his employment under the War- rington British Workman Public-house Company. He did not think that the bench would call a man of that description a right and proper person to receive a license to sell drink off the premises. He (Mr. Roberts) could have asked questions with reference to the time when he was a licensee, but he thought perhaps what he had to say upon it would be quite sufficient. With reference to the general grounds of objection, he believed that there were in this borough, something like 205 licenses in operation. There were 66 fully licensed houses, 45 beer licenses, and 74 licenses to sell off the premises. Taking the population of Warrington at 62,000 or 63,000, there was one l:censee tor every 250 of the population. Take any 250 people in Warringtcn, 150 would be children. A hundred adults was a very liberal allowance. He would therefore say that only 100 out of the 250 required drink at all, and tor every 100 adults in this town, there was one license. It seemed to him that not one of those would have to travel far before he was enabled to slack his fiery thirst. There were also 86 places fully licensed, and therefore anyone would have an opportunity of getting spirits. An objection might be made that the whole of the tAown was taken. He would, therefore, localise it. In the neighbourhood of that place for which the application was made, there were two licenses very near. He disputed the witness's distances and that gentleman had not stated that he had measured them. With regard to the application of Mr. Kenyon, he would inform their worships that the Bowl- ing Green Inn was not more that 60 or 70 yards away. He objected to the wine license being granted because he was told on the best authority that there was a sort of an idea amongst workingmen—how it could possibly have originated, he did not know—which was to the effect that wine was a teetotal drink, and therefore it was just possible that the facilities for obtaining that liquor would increase unmigakeably and unconsciously the habit of drinking. With regard to the off-license of Mr. Johnson, he would say that there were four off- • licenses in the immediate neighbourhood, as there were William Allen, Bramhall-st., William Throssall, Lovely. lane, Martha Ann Potter, Selby-st., and .1. W. Jones, Cartwright-st. The figures which Mr. Browne gave were simply his opinion, and he (Mr. Roberts) had an equal rialit to give his opinion. He believed that out-door licenses were sources of great danger owing to children being sent by their parents to them, and thus acquirin

the habit of going for drink. Parents sent their children to off-licessed houses, who would not send them to the public-house, and thus habits might be acquired which would in the long run tend to their ruin. As to the question of local option he thought that that question had been soundly condemned by popular opinion— (laughter)—and as their worships were the persons who had the power, be aAred them to exercise it, and he confidently looked to them to refuse the license.

The Ctiief Constable said that he felt that they had already enough off-licenses in Warrington. He had sent Inspectors Spinks and Cox to inspect the distances be- tween that shop and other licensed premises as he thought that their worships would wish for some opinion as to the distances. As far as Mr. Kenyon was con- cerned, he never opposed an application of that sort, as he thought that a wine license raised the tone of the house.

Inspector Spinks was then called. He said that John- son's place was in Wellfield-street at the corner of Percy- street, and Mr. Throssall's premises were in Lovely-lane right opposite the end of Percy-street, and were 150 yards away from such other. In the whole neighbourhood in a radius of 600 yards from the applicant's premises, there were three fully licensed houses, one beer house (Kenyon's) and ten off licenses. Potter's house was 220 yards away, the Green Man 420, and the Bowling Green 520 yards.—By Mr. Browne : He did not think that the inhabitants in the neighbourhood of Wellfield-street would go into Cart- wright-street or Priestley-street for beer.—By Mr. Roberts ; The Bowling Green Inn was 100 yards from Mr. Kenyon's house, and the Ship Inn, 140 yards. Inspector Cox gave corroborative evidence. —. •
The tnacistrales then retired and in *about two minutes, they returned, and the Mayor announced that they had refused both applications. The sessions were then adjourned until September 27th.

BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO , LIMITED.
HALF-YEARLY MEETING.

The twenty-ninth half-yearly meeting of the above company was held on Thursday at the Law Association- rooms, Cook-street, Liverpool. Sir J. T. Brunner,M.P., presided over a good attendance of shareholders. The half-yearly report showed a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working. of the half-year ended on the 30th of June, 1895. of £148,762 14s. 7d. which, with the amount of £89,117 15s. 6d. brought for- ward front the previous half-year, made a total of £237,880 103. id. The directors proposed to deal with the above balance as follows :—Dividend on the prefer- ence capital at 7 per cent, per annum,£ls,22s ; dividend on the ordinary capital, at 30 per cent, per annum, £129.856 24 6L; amount to be written off patents account. £2,500; halance to be carried forward, £90,299 7s. 7d.—total, £237,880 109. id. The directors had pur- chased the lands, works, and business of Murgatroyd's Ammonia Soda and Salt Syndicate, Limited, of Middle- wich (exclusive of their salt works and business), as a going concern as from the Ist inst., on advantageous terms. The directors contemplated making a call of £1 per share on the ordinary shares, now £2 103. paid, to become due on the Ist of October next.

The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report and the declaration of the dividends, said the dividends were the same as those paid for several half-years past. It would be noticed that the directors had purchased Murgatrovd's works on a ivantageons terms to the corn- pany,and he asked to be ex,msed naming the price paid, as it was not to the advantage of the company that it should he made known. Applications for the new issue of 6,000 preference shares were to be in by the 29th inst. They had already exceeded the number to ba issued, a fact which was very satisfactory to those who had the prosperity of the company at heart. Mr. Ludwig Mond seconded, and doubted if any shareholder expected better results during the past half- year, tor everyone who had followed the alkali trade knew that the prices had constantly been going down, , and had been lower during the last halt-year than ever , before.

Mr. Newman inquired how the sum of £277.000 men- tioned in the report under the head of investments was invested. He also asked how the new shares would rank with the existing ones, because as they might not always have 30 per cent, it was important to know in what rotation they came. He would also like to know the necessity for issuing new shares when only £2 10s. had been called up on those in existence. The Chairman replied that the investments consisted partly of a considerable share in a company of the same character as their own, but the bulk were in the cate- gory of trustees' securities. The new preference shares they were now issuing would stand exactly on a par with the preference shares now existing. Mr. Newman.—They will come after the 'ordinary shares. The Chairman said they would come before the ordi- nary shares. They bad issued these shares for the bene- fit of the ordinary shares. As a matter of course, preference shares were always issued for the benefit of the ordinary shares, in order that the possessor of ordi- naly shares might make money out of the transaction. As 0 Mr. Newman's fears that they might not always have 30 per cent., he thought the owners of the prefer- ence shares might calculate upon having 7. (Laughter.) Replying to another question put by a shareholder, the Chairman further stated that all applications for the new issue received by the 29th inst. would rank together,and those entitled to allotments would have them if their applications came in time. The report and declaration of dividends were unani- mously agreed to. On the motion of Mr. Jones, seconded by Mr. Irvine, the sum of £6OO was voted to the directors other than the managing directors, for their services 'for the half year,and on the motion of Mr.Gallovvay,seconded by Mr. Holland, a vote of thanks was accorded to the managers and staffs for their efficiency and diligence. Thanks to the Chairman t gininated the meeting.

THE REV. ISAAC PHILLIPS, LATE OF ORFORD. It will be a matter of interest to many to hear that the Rev. Isaac Phillips, who for several years held the chaplaincy at Orford, has accepted the curacy of St. Cuthbert's Parish Church, Lytham, in succession to the Rev. Charles Billington, the new Vicar of Knuzden, near Blackburn. Since leaving Orford in 1893 Mr. Phi:lips has for some time acted as curate at St. John's Church, Blackburn, and has just entered on his new duties. DIOCESAN PUPIL TEACHERS' EXAMINATION. In the class lists of the examination of pupil teachers in religious knowledge in the diocese of Liverpool, just issued by the Rev. F. F. Grensted, the Diocesan Inspector, among the names in Class I. prizewinners is the name of Mr. Arthur Grounds, one of the pupil teachers at the Orforsl Day Schools, and eldest 808 of Mr. Charles Grounds, of Orford. The examiner states in his report that the results of the June examination are distinctly good, and that the steady training year by year is having a most beneficial effect. DARESBURY SCHOOL BOARD MEETING. A special meeting of the School Board was held on Friday afternoon in the Board-room for the pur- pose of appointing a mistress at the Moore Infants' School in place of Miss Round, who is leaving the district. There were present Messrs. Peter Tickle (nehmen), C. W. Phillips, A. Broome, John Cooper, Peter Gleave, and C. E. Linaker (clerk). Miss Jebb, of Derby, by araangement meL the Board, and ulti- mately it was unanimously agreed that she be ap- pointed mistress at a salary of £5O per annum, to commence duties at the beginning of the Christmas quarter. CHESHIRE DAIRY SCHOLARSHIPS. Dairy scholarships tenable for nine weeks at the Dairy Institute, Worleston have been awarded by the Cheshire County Council to the following candidates: -Miss A. Moreton, The Moss, North- WiCh Miss M. Boffey, Old Hall, Barthomley ; Miss Kate Lowe, Sutton Hall, Warriugton ; Miss Eleanor Bate, Sutton Weaver; Miss E. Holland, Broken Cross. Macclesfield ; Miss E.Powell,Hulme Waltield ; Miss R. E. Nield, Wrenbury ; Miss N. Edwards, Haslington ; Miss Lucy Heeler, liatherton, Nant- wich ; Miss Mary Clowes, Crewe: Miss Davies, Hollinfare, Warrington; Miss Pattie Thompson, Cuddingtun. UNUSUAL FATALITY TO A BOY. At the Parade room of the Police Court on Tues- day, Mr. S.Brighouse, county coroner,conducted an enquiry relative to the death of Frank Ellis, 19, Howard-st., aged six years, who died at his parents' residence on the Monday. A boy named John Thompson stated that he was with the deceased on Saturday and they were playing outside a shop in Powys-st.,when Ellis shut his eyes and commenced to run backwards. In doing so his head collided with a gaslamp with such force as to throw him to the ground. Deceased's sister,who was in the shop, took him home as he was crying. Further evidence showing that deceased complained of being ill im- mediately on reaching home and rapidly worsened, Was given by Sarah Ellen Ellis,sister of deceased,his father and mother, and Mrs. Kirkham, a neighbour. Dr. Adams certified that death was due to concus- sion of the brain.-The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." MR. SCOTT'S ELECTION EXPENSES. The election expenses of Mr. P. B. Scott at the recent election have now been filed by Mr. John Clayton, his election agent, and the total amount tomes to £594 08. Si. Mr. Scott's share of the Re- taining Officer's charges was .Clll is. 11d. His personal expenses came to .C 8 12s. 91 Mr. Clayton has received £25 for his services. Niue polling agents received 10s. 61. each ; there was paid to clerks £6B ss. 6i.; to messengers, .C 25 18s.; for printing £ll6 28. 6d.; for advertising, £79 19s. Id.; stationery, £25 13s. 11d. ; postages and telegrams, £63 12s. 81. ; hire of rooms for public meetings, £l6 148. 6d. ; and hire of committee rooms, .CI6 ss. Miscellaneous items amount to ..£32 Os. 7d. Mr. Pierpoint's election expenses,it will be remembered, were .C6lO 9s. 11d. The limit for a borough like Warrington is £5OO exclusive of Returning Officer's charges and the candidate's personal expenses. Mr. Pierpoint's personal expenses were only Bs. At the last election in 1892, Mr. Pierpoint's election ex- penses came to .C 619 14s. 21.,nearly £.9 more than on this occasion' and Dr. Houston's £615 Is. 10d. At the election, Mr. Pierpoint received 4,001 votes to Mr. Scott 3,326, 80 that each vote cost Mr. Pierpoint 3. Op., while each vote recorded for Mr. Scott cost Sc. el. LOCAL SUCCESSES AT THE OXFORD LOCAL EXAMINATIONS. In the Division lists in the Oxford local examina- tions, just published appear the names of the tollowing local students who have been successful : S Kidd, of Warrington Grammar School, was placed 7th in the list of senior candidates,first class, out of 29 candidates in the honours list. In the third class are the names of Miss W. M. Harry and Miss M. B. North, St. blphin's Clergy Daughter's School. In the pass list are the names of IL Gibson, Warrington Grammar School and Misses H. M. Giles, M. L. Norris and C. M. Phillips, Clergy Daughters' Sshool. Junior candidates,second class, 161 candidates: W. T. Gornall (102nd), and D. C. Wallace (149th), Warrington Grammar Schooi M. C. Holditch, St. Elphin's Clergy Daughters' School, Warrington ; H. M. Shurrock, Highfield School, Tarvin. Second Division, E. Gieave, Warrington, private tuition, T. Porter, Warrington Grammar School; E. M. Ash, J. G. Johnstone, and E. E. M. 'J sues, St. Elphin's Clergy Daughter's School, Warrington. GENERAL WOoLFE ANGLING SOCIETY. The fourteenth annual festival on Saturday of the General Woolfe Angling Society was one of the most successful ever experienced by that organize- ;son owing to the favourable weather. The two hours' drive to Vale Royal, the avenue selected for the competition, was thoroughly enjoyed, and the sixty members who comprised the party formed a merry group. A start was made at two o'clock, and Mr. E. Connor's break was requisitioned, Vale Royal being reached a little after four. The Navi- gation Inn was made the headquarters for the after- noon, and punctually at five . o'clock the first rod was thrown. The catches exceeded previous years, and with Mr. W. Jenks officiating as judge, this gentleman's high knowledge of the sport rendered matters agreeable,and the whole of the proceedings passed off without demur. The prizes were a hand- some lot, and were both ornamental and useful. the fifty competitors who participated in the contest all receiving some article of value. The leading tradesmen of the town contributed the whole of the handsome collection, which comprised tea services, copper kettles, knives and forks, clocks, china sets, macintosh, pipes, B..sc. After the match was over the company repaired to their headquar- ters, where refreshments were partaken of, atter which a social evening was spent, and the company at nine o'clock started for home, which was reached at eleven o'clock, all expressing themselves as hav- ing thoroughly enjoyed the outing. The presenta- tion of prizes took place on Monday evening, alter which another enjoyable time was spent,so that the season may be said to have wound up in first-class _style. Thanks to the donors and the usual toasts were duly given and honoured, and the company separated at eleven o'clock. A BOOK FOR MARRIED WOMEN. The information contained in this book ought to be known by every married woman, aud it will not harm the unmarriep to read. The book is conveniently divided into 12 chapters The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty, or when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out the best age for marriage, and who should have children and who not, and furnishes useful information that one can ordinarily get only from an intelligent doctor. The third chapter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter or treats of the signs of pregnancy. The fifth chapter tells w a woman should live during the pregnant state. Toe sixth chapter treats of mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats of maternal impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due longings t n the part of the mother, but rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy coninements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic physician says that confinements can be made comparatively easy i certain rules are obeyed ; these rules are given. The nint chapter treats of the proper management of confinement until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat the mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh chapter treats of sterility ; gives the main causes of it, how these may be overcome and children result The last chapter treats of the "change," a most important article for all women over forty. The book is full of useful information and no book is written which goes so thoroughly into matters relating to married women. Some may think too much is told ; such can scarcely be the cam. for knowledge is power and the means of attaining happiness. 'lhe book can be ha from Dr. T. R.
